properties.description: Cognition introduced SWE-2 in September 2026, a coding model post-trained from Kimi K3 and available in Devin Desktop and the Devin CLI. Test one job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What SWE-2 is

Cognition introduced SWE-2 as its most advanced coding model, the successor to SWE-1.7. The post is Introducing SWE-2. Cognition says SWE-2 scores 50.0 percent on FrontierCode 1.1 Main, within about one point of Fable 5.1, and that it is 64 percent cheaper on that comparison. It also says the model was post-trained from Kimi K3, and that the training covered every reasoning-effort level in one run so the cost and quality tradeoff moved together.

SWE-2 is available in Devin Desktop and the Devin CLI. Cognition says it is also rolling out on Devin Web and Fusion. This is a coding-agent model inside Cognition's products. It is not a general chat model for resident mail, and it is not an innflow feature.

On behavior, Cognition says the medium effort setting explores less and edits sooner than SWE-1.7, which users had found too slow to start. It reports better end-to-end tests and a habit of checking a claim instead of agreeing with it. Those observations come from Cognition's own runs. They are a reason for a developer to try SWE-2 on a repo, not a property-operations benchmark.

Coding help is still a pull request

A stronger coding model can draft a reconciliation script, a report exporter, or a fix in an internal tool. The merge still belongs to a person who can run the tests. SWE-2 does not get production credentials, and it does not get a path that messages residents.

Cost claims on FrontierCode are about that benchmark's tasks. Your repo is the test that counts: does the patch pass, and how many review comments does it attract?

Keep it out of the property system of record

innflow does not have a Cognition or the Cognition model key. Do not describe a native integration that does not exist. A developer can use Devin on a codebase. The resulting change arrives like any other change, through review.

Property data stays in the property management system. If a script written with the Cognition model reads an export, the export is a copy and the script's output is a proposal. A person checks it before anything is posted. The same rule covers vendors and owners: the model does not send the email.

A bounded trial

Give the Cognition model one repository and one class of task, such as small bug fixes with tests already in place. Compare it with the coding model the team used last month on time-to-first-correct-patch, not on a demo. Stop if it needs broad write access to look good.

the Cognition model is a coding release for people who already work in Devin. It can help build tools around property operations. It should not operate the books or the inbox.

When the approved step needs a home, use innflow.

Devin Web and Fusion are a rollout, not a promise that every seat has the Cognition model today. Check the picker in the product you actually use. If the ID is missing, the announcement is news, not a tool your team can assign on Monday morning.

Keep the Cognition model inside the coding seat you already pay for. It is not a model you drop into an innflow node by pasting a key, because innflow has no Cognition key slot. If a developer wants it for a lease-abstraction script or a reconciliation helper, the output still comes back as a draft. A coordinator checks names, dates, and amounts against the property management system before anyone relies on them. That split keeps a stronger coding model useful without turning Devin into the system of record. Give the trial one repository, one written task, and a person who can run the tests.

Write the model ID, the price you observed, and the pass rule in one note the on-call person can open.

Review the first ten outputs with the person who owns the queue before the volume goes up.

properties.description: StepFun released Step 5 Preview on September 20, 2026: a 600 billion model, 1 million token context, API access now, weights planned October 15. Test one job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
A preview, with a date for the weights

StepFun introduced Step 5 Preview on September 20, 2026 as its flagship for agentic work. The company points it at software engineering, professional knowledge work, and finance, and says the goal is strong performance at a lower task cost. The page is Step 5 Preview. It is a preview. Call it that.

StepFun describes a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 600 billion parameters total and 27 billion active per token, a 1 million token context window, and vision input. The hosted model is available through StepFun products and the API under the ID step-5-preview. Open weights are promised for October 15, 2026. Until that date, self-hosting is not an option. Documentation cited by launch coverage lists text, image, and video input, text output, and reasoning effort of low, medium, or high, plus tool calling and structured output.

API rates reported from StepFun's docs are about $1 per million input tokens, about $0.05 per million on a cache hit, and $2.70 per million output tokens. Check the live price page before you rely on those figures. Launch-week numbers move.

Finance strength is not a property ledger

StepFun highlights finance among the workloads. That is their evaluation story. It is not a statement that Step 5 Preview understands your chart of accounts, your trust accounting rules, or your owner's distribution schedule. A model that is strong on a lab's finance set can still invent a late fee.

Long context is useful for a thick file. It is also how a prompt gets expensive. Retrieve the pages you need. Do not paste the entire closing binder because the window allows it.

No native StepFun switch

innflow does not have a StepFun key slot. Do not tell a team that Step 5 Preview is built in. If a gateway you already use lists step-5-preview, test it there and name the gateway in the runbook. Open weights, when they arrive in October, are a separate project: hosting, not a checkbox.

Until then, keep experiments off resident communication. The property management system remains the system of record. A person approves every message to a resident, an owner, or a vendor. A visual workflow can hold the draft and the approval next to each other so the preview model never becomes the sender.

What to wait for

If you need a stable ID with a contract, wait. If you want a look at the preview, use one internal coding or extraction task with a known answer. Revisit the choice when the October 15 weights are actually public, and when you can see whether the API price held.

Step 5 Preview is a real hosted model with a published architecture and a promised weight release. It is not yet a default for daily property operations.

A starting point is the Qwen blog: Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash.

Those are Qwen's figures. International list prices reported from Alibaba Cloud around the launch were about $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.47 per million output tokens, with different rates by region and by input type. Read the console for your region before you quote a number.

The model is served as an API. Do not assume open weights. Alongside it, Qwen published tooling so text agent harnesses can accept audio and video. That is a developer detail. It is not a property feature by itself.

Audio and video are a different workload

A text model that drafts from a lease PDF is not the same tool as a model that listens to a maintenance voicemail or watches a unit walkthrough. Qwen 3.8 Omni-Flash is interesting for the second job: meeting notes, a long inspection video, a call recording a manager already has the right to store. It is a poor place to invent a policy from a clip.

Keep recordings you are allowed to process. Do not expand collection because a model can now hear them. A longer context window is not consent.

A Qwen key is supported. The new ID still needs a check.

innflow supports a Qwen key under Settings, then BYOK. The key is an encrypted secret. Selecting Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash, or any other Qwen 3.8 ID, is a separate choice on the node. Older Qwen workflows should stay on their current ID until you compare outputs.

Use the model to summarize material a person will read. Do not let it tell a resident the outcome of a dispute. The property management system holds the official record. Permission gates keep outbound messages with a person.

Pick one ID and one job

Choose either a text task or an audio task for the pilot, not both. Twenty real examples are enough to see whether names, amounts, and dates survive. If the model summarizes a video well and mangles a ledger, keep it on the video.

Qwen 3.8 is a family in motion. Omni-Flash is the September piece worth a careful test. Name the ID in the runbook so the next family release does not silently replace it.

Get started with innflow when the summary needs a person in the loop.

Regional price tables for Qwen 3.8 do not match each other. Quote the region you deploy in, and date the quote. A number from a Singapore console is not a Beijing number. Rebuild the estimate when you change regions instead of averaging them.

The model, not the coding app

Meta released Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026. The post says it improves agentic and coding work and is easier to use in real settings after months of Muse Code and Meta Model API adoption. Muse Spark 1.3 with max reasoning is available in Muse Code and on the Meta Model API. The announcement is Introducing Muse Spark 1.3. This is the model. It is not the Muse Code product, and it is not a realtime avatar.

Meta describes a model trained to stay with longer tasks, to use tools when sources conflict, and to keep track of what it has learned. It says Muse Spark 1.3 asks clarifying questions when a prompt is ambiguous, asks for help when it is stuck, and confirms before consequential actions. It also says the model follows long instructions more reliably than earlier Muse Spark models and is better at knowing what it does not know. Those are Meta's claims about training. Test them on your files.

The official post does not publish a token price in the body reviewed here. Do not invent one. Read the API pricing page for the ID you will call before you estimate a month of use.

Confirmation before action is the useful habit

A model that asks before it takes a consequential step is aligned with how property work should run. The confirmation still has to land on a person, not on another model turn. "Consequential" in an operations queue includes sending a notice, changing a balance, scheduling entry, and promising a vendor.

Long-horizon skill is also how a workflow drifts. A model that works for an hour can bury a wrong assumption under a polished deliverable. Ask it to show the source lines. Do not accept the finished memo alone.

No native Muse key

innflow does not have a Meta Muse key slot. Muse Spark 1.3 is not a built-in model. A developer can use Muse Code or the Meta Model API on their own. Bringing the result into a property workflow means pasting a draft into a reviewed step, not flipping a toggle.

The property management system stays the system of record. A visual canvas can hold the draft next to the approval. Residents, owners, and vendors are contacted by a person. That is true for Muse Spark 1.3 and for every other model on this board.

One ambiguous task is the test

Give Muse Spark 1.3 a messy assignment with missing facts, the kind that should produce a question rather than a guess. If it invents the missing number, it is not ready for that queue. If it asks and then drafts from the answer you provide, you have a candidate for internal drafting.

Muse Spark 1.3 is a September model update for longer agent work. Use the questions it asks. Do not skip the person who answers them.

Keep that person on the workflow with innflow.

This release is also not the avatar product some teams already know from Meta. If a colleague says "Muse," ask whether they mean this model, Muse Code, or a realtime avatar. The three are easy to mix up, and only one of them is the September 2 model release.

Ask for the model ID in writing before a pilot starts. Muse Code can host more than one generation, and a teammate may still be on the prior Spark release. Run the same clarifying-question task on both if both are available, and keep the one that asks a useful question instead of stalling. Do not connect the result to resident messaging. A person confirms consequential actions, which is the behavior the release notes themselves emphasize, and the property management system remains the record. There is no Meta key slot in innflow, so this model is not a native node.

What MiniMax shipped

MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a preview, not a fully priced public API launch. On September 27, 2026, MiniMax turned MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-Preview on inside MiniMax Code and made it available to Token Plan subscribers. The company's own note is short: it is built for everyday development, from quick bug fixes to full features. There was no benchmark report and no pay-as-you-go rate card with this preview.

What is public is the shape of the product. Reporting on MiniMax's materials describes a context window of up to 1 million tokens, with text, image, and video input. Inside MiniMax Code, reasoning effort can be set to low, medium, high, xhigh, or max. Higher effort means a longer wait and more output tokens. Thinking stays on. MiniMax has not published a parameter count for this preview.

That is a different kind of release from a flagship with a model card. MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a product toggle first. Teams that do not use MiniMax Code or a Token Plan cannot assume they can call it from a generic API key today. Treat any third-party listing with care until MiniMax publishes a stable endpoint and a price.

Why a quiet preview still matters

Coding agents are how a lot of internal tools get built: a delinquency export, a owner-statement checker, a small script that files vendor invoices. A preview model can be useful for a developer who already lives in that vendor's app. It is a weak choice for a workflow that has to run every morning without a person watching the model picker.

The absence of a published score is information. You do not have a lab number to quote to an owner. You have a product you can try on your own tickets. That is the right standard anyway. A benchmark from another lab's coding suite will not tell you whether the model respects your chart of accounts.

What innflow does and does not connect

innflow does not have a native MiniMax key slot. Supported bring-your-own-key providers are OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, Kimi, and Qwen, plus a few search tools. Do not describe MiniMax M3.1 Flash as a built-in innflow model.

If a gateway you already pay for lists the preview later, test it there. Until then, the honest setup is a person using MiniMax Code for a draft, then bringing the result back to a reviewed workflow. The property management system stays the system of record. Nothing goes to a resident, owner, or vendor until a person sends it.

A practical test

If someone on the team has MiniMax Code, give them one internal script that is already specified: inputs, outputs, and the tests that define done. Compare the preview with the model that script uses now. Keep production runs on the model that has a price, an ID, and a week of clean reviews.

MiniMax M3.1 Flash is worth knowing about because it is live for subscribers. It is not yet a default for property operations. Wait for a stable API and a price before you attach it to a daily process.

For workflows that already have a review step, start with innflow.

Token Plan prices are subscription prices, not a per-token rate for this preview. A developer on that plan can try MiniMax M3.1 Flash on a side project. A finance lead should not forecast API spend from a plan that does not publish one. Wait for the rate card.

Write down what you were allowed to try. MiniMax M3.1 Flash was announced for people already inside MiniMax Code and the Token Plan. A colleague with a personal login is not a company rollout. There is no MiniMax key in innflow settings, so this preview does not appear as a native node. If a gateway lists the preview ID later, test one coding task with a known answer and keep the transcript. Until then, the honest status is a subscriber preview without a public per-token price. Reported context and effort levels are secondary descriptions, not a scorecard MiniMax published on a model card.

properties.description: Xiaomi released MiMo 2.6 Pro and Flash in late September 2026 under an MIT license, with open weights and a 1 million token window. Test one scoped job.

properties.draft_blog:
Two models under one card

The card says MiMo 2.6. Xiaomi shipped a pair, not a single checkpoint. Around September 21 and 22, 2026, it released MiMo-V2.6-Pro and MiMo-V2.6-Flash with MIT-licensed weights and a public technical report. The product page is MiMo-V2.6. Treat the announcement as the pair.

Reporting on Xiaomi's model card describes Pro as a mixture-of-experts model of about 1.02 trillion parameters, with about 42 billion active per token. Flash is described as about 309 billion total and about 15 billion active. Both are described with a 1 million token context window and input that includes text, images, video, and audio, with text output. Hosted access has been reported through Xiaomi's API, AI Studio, MiMo Code, MiMo Desktop, and OpenRouter.

List prices cited from Xiaomi's own endpoint are about $0.435 per million input tokens and $0.87 per million output tokens for Pro, and about $0.14 and $0.28 for Flash. A faster Pro UltraSpeed option has been listed at about ten times the Pro rate. Confirm the live price before you budget. Open weights mean a team can also self-host, which is a different cost: machines, not tokens.

Open weights change the review, not the rules

An MIT license means you may run the weights yourself. It does not mean the model is correct about a security deposit or a vendor's insurance. Self-hosting is attractive when data cannot leave your network. It is extra work when you only needed a draft.

Pro is the candidate for harder agent tasks. Flash is the candidate for volume. Do not collapse them into one setting called MiMo 2.6 in a runbook. The ID you call is the thing you are evaluating.

What this means in innflow

There is no Xiaomi key field in innflow settings. Supported keys include OpenRouter. If MiMo 2.6 Pro or Flash is listed on OpenRouter, that is the path to try, using the OpenRouter node, not a claim that innflow ships a native MiMo toggle.

Private or VPC deployment of innflow is a separate question from where the model runs. If the model is called through a third-party router, prompts go to that router. Say that plainly in the review. The property management system still holds the books. A person still approves anything sent to a resident, an owner, or a vendor.

How to evaluate the pair

Pick one internal task with an answer key. Run Flash and Pro on the same twenty items. Record cost, time, and corrections. If Flash is close enough, do not pay Pro prices out of habit. If both invent amounts, neither is ready.

MiMo 2.6 is an open pair with a real license and a low list price. It is ready to test. It is not a reason to skip the approval step.

Put the approval on the canvas with innflow.

Self-hosting MiMo 2.6 is a capacity project, not a Friday task. Pro is a trillion-parameter class model. If you do not already run that kind of stack, use a hosted endpoint and treat the weights as an option for later, after someone owns the machines and the updates.

If you consume MiMo 2.6 through OpenRouter, say so in the runbook. the innflow OpenRouter node is the honest path, because there is no Xiaomi key slot in Settings. Confirm the exact ID, Pro or Flash, before a workflow runs. Pro and Flash are different sizes and different prices, and a teammate who says the family name has not picked one. Hosted calls still need the same review as any other model. A person checks resident, owner, and vendor messages, and the property management system keeps the ledger. List prices quoted from the V2.5 card should be checked on the day you switch.

properties.description: Inception released Mercury 2.5 on September 8, 2026, a diffusion model it clocks at 1,107 tokens per second, listed at $0.20 and $0.75 per million. Confirm it.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What Inception shipped

Inception's blog lists Mercury 2.5 on September 8, 2026. The company calls it a diffusion language model, the most capable one it has put in production, and says it is the largest diffusion language model it knows of. The post is Introducing Mercury 2.5. Inception says quality rose about 40 percent versus Mercury 2, with the same low-latency serving style.

The published specs are direct. Speed is 1,107 tokens per second on widely available NVIDIA GPUs, by Inception's measure. Context is 260,000 tokens. List price is $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.75 per million output tokens. At launch, Inception offered 80 percent off, at $0.04 and $0.15 per million. A promo price is not the price you should put in a yearly plan. Capabilities called out in the post include tunable reasoning, parallel tool calls, and schema-aligned JSON.

Mercury 2.5 is available through the Inception API, Baseten, and OpenRouter. The same post previews Mercury Voice, with time to first token under 170 milliseconds, and Mercury Router, which sends a prompt to other models. Those are previews, not the main model.

Speed is the point, and the point has a limit

Inception describes search, voice, and coding products that call a model many times inside one user action. That is where a fast, cheap model earns its place: rewriting a query, compacting a long note, routing a request. Inception cites customers, including a voice company and a coding tool, with large latency cuts. Those are the company's examples. Repeat them as such.

A fast model is a weak place to make a final decision about money. Use Mercury 2.5 for the small steps around a decision. Use a person, or a stronger reviewed step, for the decision itself.

OpenRouter is the path, not a native switch

innflow does not have an Inception key field. It does support an OpenRouter key, and Inception says Mercury 2.5 is on OpenRouter. That is the honest route: the OpenRouter node, aimed at the Mercury ID, if the router still lists it. Do not describe a first-party Mercury toggle.

Even on a fast model, the property management system stays the system of record. A canvas step can classify or summarize. A permission gate holds messages to residents, owners, and vendors. Speed does not skip the gate.

Where to try it

Put Mercury 2.5 on one helper step you can time: shortening a thread before a person reads it, or turning a messy note into fields. Compare latency and correction rate with the helper you use now. Leave resident calls alone until a voice preview is a product you have actually tested, with a disclosure.

Mercury 2.5 is a diffusion model sold on speed and price. Use it where those two things are the requirement, and keep the commitment with a person.

Start with innflow for the step a person still has to approve.

The launch discount of 80 percent is a temporary price. Budget the list rate of $0.20 and $0.75 per million tokens, and treat the discount as a bonus if it is still on the invoice. A helper step that only works while it is nearly free is not a helper you can keep.

Diffusion is a different serving shape, not a different approval rule. A fast draft is still a draft. Time the call on your own packet, because 1,107 tokens per second is the company figure, measured on their setup. Then time the human review. If the review takes minutes, the generation speed is not the bottleneck. Use the OpenRouter node in innflow when the listing shows this model, and record the price you were actually charged, including whether the launch discount was still applied. Customer stories on the company blog are examples from Inception, not results from your portfolio.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: SpaceXAI released Grok 4.7 on September 21, 2026. Under 200,000 prompt tokens it is $2 input and $6 output per million, with a 500k window. Test one job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What Grok 4.7 is

SpaceXAI released Grok 4.7 on September 21, 2026. The company calls it its most capable model for coding and knowledge work: longer runs on hard tasks, more careful self-checks, and its best-calibrated safeguards so far. It is served at the same price and speed as Grok 4.6. The announcement is Introducing Grok 4.7. The API name is grok-4.7.

The docs list a 500,000 token context window, a knowledge cutoff of May 2026, text and image input, and text output. Reasoning effort is low, medium, high, or xhigh, and it cannot be turned off. The default is high. Below 200,000 prompt tokens, the API price is $2 per million input tokens, $0.50 per million cached input tokens, and $6 per million output tokens. At or above 200,000 prompt tokens, the whole request is billed at $4, $1, and $12. A fast variant costs twice the standard rates and is limited to Cursor and Grok Build. It is not on the public API.

SpaceXAI also says Grok 4.7 was trained to understand the Grok Bot harness. On the launch post, its own table shows CursorBench 4.0 at 46.3 percent, against 40.4 percent for Grok 4.6, 41.7 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 51.8 percent for Fable 5.1. DeepSWE v1.1 is listed at 71.0 percent for Grok 4.7 at high effort. Those are vendor scores. Quote them as SpaceXAI's numbers.

Long context has a price step

A 500,000 token window is large enough to hold a thick lease file plus a thread. The price doubles once the prompt crosses 200,000 tokens, and it doubles for every token in that request, not only the extra ones. Stuffing a whole portfolio into one call is often the expensive way to use Grok 4.7. Summaries and retrieval usually cost less than one giant prompt.

The fast variant is a product choice inside Cursor or Grok Build, billed there. Do not plan an API budget around it.

Using a Grok key in property work

innflow accepts a Grok key under Settings, then BYOK. Saving the key does not flip existing workflows to grok-4.7. Select the ID on the node, and watch the prompt size if you care about the 200,000 token step.

Coding help and draft knowledge work are the fit. Posting charges is not. The property management system stays the system of record. On the canvas, a permission gate keeps resident, owner, and vendor messages with a person. Keys are stored encrypted, and the settings page shows only the last four characters.

A fair test

Compare Grok 4.7 with the model you use for the same coding or drafting job, at the effort level you would actually pay for. High is the default, and it is not free thinking. If xhigh does not change the acceptance rate, do not leave it on.

Grok 4.7 is a documented API model with a clear price schedule. Use the schedule. Then keep the approval where a person can see it.

Start with innflow to put that approval on the workflow.

Reasoning effort changes the bill because reasoning tokens are billed. High is the default. Try medium on the classification step before you accept high as the habit. Keep xhigh for the rare job where medium and high both fail the rubric.

The price changes at 200,000 prompt tokens, and the higher rate applies to the whole request, not only the tokens past the line. A long lease packet can cross that line without anyone noticing. Trim the packet, or accept the higher rate on purpose. Fast mode is a separate serving path in Cursor and Grok Build. It is not a flag on the public API, so a Grok key in innflow does not turn it on. Use the standard slot for the public model, and write down whether the prompt sits under or over the long-context line. Benchmark rows on the announcement are the vendor numbers. Grade your own job beside them.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: OpenAI put GPT-Live-1 in the API on September 10, 2026. The voice layer is $0.05 a minute and can listen and speak at the same time. Test one scoped job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
A voice model, separate from the text models

On September 10, 2026, OpenAI released GPT-Live-1 in the API. It is a full-duplex voice model: it can listen and speak at the same time, and it can hand deeper reasoning and actions to another model. OpenAI distinguishes that front end from the backend you pair it with. The announcement is GPT-Live-1 in the API. It is not GPT Realtime 2.1, and it is not a transcription-only product.

The voice layer is priced at $0.05 per minute. Backend model tokens and tools are billed separately, so the real cost depends on which model does the thinking. OpenAI says interruption handling was a design point. In early evaluations it cites, Speak found that learners got more time to think and that interruptions fell by almost 80 percent versus earlier turn-based systems. That is a language-tutoring result from a launch partner. It is not a call-center guarantee.

GPT-Live-1 is for products that need a spoken conversation. A property team that only drafts email does not need it. A team that takes phone requests might, and the constraints are stricter than for a text draft, because a caller hears the answer immediately.

What a caller must not be promised

A voice model can collect a maintenance description, repeat a unit number, and offer to have a person call back. It should not approve a refund, waive a fee, promise an entry window, or state a balance unless that balance was read from the property management system and the script allows it. Spoken confidence is not a ledger.

Recording and notice rules are local. A new API does not change them. If you cannot say, on the call, that the caller is talking with an automated system, do not place the model on the line.

An OpenAI key is not a phone product

innflow can store an OpenAI key under Settings, then BYOK, for supported model nodes. That is not the same as shipping a GPT-Live-1 phone agent. Do not imply that saving a key turns on outbound or inbound resident calls. Voice, if you pilot it, belongs in a system built for calls, with a disclosure, a handoff, and a log.

Text workflows stay the default for this stack. Drafts sit on a visual canvas. A person sends anything that goes to a resident, an owner, or a vendor. The property management system remains the system of record after the call, not the transcript alone.

If you pilot voice, keep it small

One inbound line, business hours, a script that can only create a request for a person to handle. Listen to the first twenty calls. Count wrong unit numbers and any promise the script did not allow. Turn it off if either number is ugly.

GPT-Live-1 is a real API for natural voice, with a simple per-minute voice price and a separate thinking bill. Use it only where a person can still own the commitment.

For the work that stays in text and review, start with innflow.

Write the handoff sentence into the script: the caller can leave a request, and a person will confirm anything that costs money or grants access. GPT-Live-1 can say that sentence. It should not improvise a better one. Review the recording for improvisation, not only for politeness.

Full duplex is a product behavior, not a permission to place calls. GPT-Live-1 can listen and speak at once inside an application someone builds on the API. innflow does not place resident calls with that model, and an OpenAI key in BYOK does not turn on a voice agent. If a vendor offers a voice demo, ask who places the call, where the recording is stored, and who confirms any promise about money or access. Those answers belong in the runbook before a single resident hears a synthetic voice. The voice-minute price and the backend model tokens are separate lines on the bill.
properties.Title: GPT-Live-1 Brings Full-Duplex Voice to the API

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: OpenAI launched GPT-6 Sol on September 22, 2026 at $2 per million input tokens and $10 output, half the GPT-5.6 Sol promotional price. Test one scoped job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
GPT-6 Sol, one week before the next Sol

OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Sol on September 22, 2026, in the same post as GPT-6 Luna. The company framed both as ways to bring frontier intelligence into everyday work after GPT-6 Astra. On September 29 it updated that post to point readers at GPT-6.1 Sol. GPT-6 Sol is still the model in the original price table. The post is here: Introducing GPT-6 Sol and Luna.

API pricing dropped 50 percent versus GPT-5.6 promotional rates. GPT-6 Sol is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, down from $4 and $20. OpenAI says the cut comes from better caching and inference, passed on to customers. the September 22 Sol model is available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users.

If you are choosing a model on September 29, read the newer GPT-6.1 Sol note before you standardize on GPT-6 Sol. The newer Sol is the one OpenAI is pointing to for agentic coding and professional work. the September 22 Sol model remains the September 22 tier, and it is the right comparison point for anyone who already moved off GPT-5.6 Sol that week.

What a 50 percent list-price cut is worth

Half the token price is real money on a workflow that runs all day: invoice coding, lease abstraction, maintenance classification. It is not a reason to widen what the model is allowed to do. A cheaper model that emails residents is a more expensive mistake, not a savings.

Compare the September 22 Sol model with the model it replaced on finished tasks. Count retries. A model that is half the price and needs twice the review is a wash. Cached prompts, which the September 29 Sol announcement discusses in more detail, are a separate lever. Do not assume the September 22 price table includes the $0.10 cached rate published for GPT-6.1 Sol.

Trying GPT-6 Sol in operations

An OpenAI key can live in innflow under Settings, then BYOK. That stores the secret. It does not select the September 22 Sol model for you. If a workflow was pinned to an older Sol ID, leave it pinned until you have a written comparison. New IDs are opt-in.

Keep the property management system as the system of record. Use the model to draft and check. Put a person in front of every message to a resident, owner, or vendor. The canvas is where that handoff is visible, so a coordinator can see what the model proposed and what was approved.

Do not skip the newer Sol

the September 22 Sol model is the mid-September price cut. GPT-6.1 Sol is the September 29 upgrade aimed closer to Astra. Teams that evaluate one should look at both, on the same ten tasks, before they lock a default for the quarter.

Price is the headline. The operating constraint is the same as last month. The ledger stays put, and a person still sends the note.

Get started with innflow if you want that handoff on the workflow itself.

If a team already moved to the September 22 Sol model on September 22, do not rip it out on September 29 because a newer Sol exists. Finish the comparison. A stable ID that people have reviewed is worth more than a launch-day swap that nobody has graded.

Half off a promotional price is still a promotional comparison. Open the current price page on the day you switch, because OpenAI has already shipped a later Sol model at its own rates. If this September 22 ID remains the one you call, record that choice so nobody upgrades a working step during a launch week. Cache pricing matters only when the prompt repeats. A unique work order on every call will not see the cached rate, and the invoice will show standard input instead. Availability in the announcement is ChatGPT Work and Codex for paid plans, not a claim about Chat or a free tier.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: GPT-6 Luna launched on September 22, 2026 at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 output, half the GPT-5.6 Luna promotional price. Test one scoped job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What GPT-6 Luna is for

GPT-6 Luna shipped on September 22, 2026 with GPT-6 Sol. OpenAI describes the pair as two balances of capability and cost under GPT-6 Astra. Luna is the inexpensive one. Input moved from $0.20 to $0.10 per million tokens. Output moved from $1.20 to $0.50. That is a 50 percent cut versus GPT-5.6 Luna promotional pricing. The source is Introducing GPT-6 Sol and Luna.

GPT-6 Luna is available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users, the same availability line OpenAI gives GPT-6 Sol. It is not the September 29 model. That update points to GPT-6.1 Sol. Luna stays the high-volume tier in the September 22 table.

Use GPT-6 Luna where the task is short, repeated, and easy to check. Sorting inbound requests, rewriting a note into a house style, or extracting fields from a clean PDF are the shape of work that belongs on a low-cost model. Multi-hour investigations and anything with legal effect belong on a stronger model, with a person reviewing the result.

Cost only helps if the error rate stays flat

At $0.50 per million output tokens, GPT-6 Luna can look almost free next to Astra-class prices. The bill that matters is the human one. If coordinators spend an extra minute fixing each draft, a portfolio of a few hundred units will erase the token savings in a week.

Run a paired test. Take 50 real items. Half go through the current cheap model, half through GPT-6 Luna. Score them on the same rubric: correct fields, no invented amounts, tone that matches the template. Keep the losers off the live queue.

Where it fits with innflow

Bring an OpenAI key into innflow at Settings, then BYOK, if you want OpenAI models on supported nodes. Confirm the node is actually set to the Luna ID. A workspace key is not a model selection.

High-volume steps are exactly where a visual workflow earns its keep. Classification can run on GPT-6 Luna. A later step can escalate odd cases to a stronger model or to a person. Messages to residents, owners, and vendors do not leave from the cheap model. The property management system remains the record of what was charged and what was promised.

Keep Luna in its lane

GPT-6 Luna is the budget GPT-6 option from September 22. It is a good candidate for repetitive drafting and extraction. It is a poor candidate for unsupervised decisions about money, access, or legal notices.

Name the lane in writing before you scale it. Then the next model launch is a swap inside that lane, not a rewrite of the process.

Build the lane at innflow.

Set a monthly cap in the place you pay the bill, even when the token price looks small. A low list price makes it easy to run a step on every inbound message. That is fine when the step is a sort. It is not fine when each message also triggers a long tool trace you did not notice.

Price the whole path, not the one model call. A sort that looks cheap can hand work to a second model, a search tool, and a person who rewrites the draft. Add those minutes before you call the low-cost tier the inexpensive choice. On a property team the usual path is a request that arrives messy, a draft that looks tidy, and a coordinator who still has to check the unit, the amount, and the date. Keep that check. A lower token price is a reason to run the check on more items, not a reason to drop it. Store the rubric next to the workflow so the next price cut does not reset the test. Cap the daily volume for the first week and read the invoice before you lift the cap.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra on September 3, 2026 as its most capable model that month, then pointed September 29 readers toward GPT-6.1 Sol. Test one job.

properties.draft_blog:
The flagship, then the pointer

OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra on September 3, 2026. The research index describes it as the company's most intelligent and aligned model yet, with state-of-the-art claims across computer use, coding, cybersecurity, and science. The post is GPT-6 Astra. Those capability claims are OpenAI's. They are not an independent scoreboard, and they are not a property-management result.

By September 29, OpenAI's newer posts point readers to GPT-6.1 Sol for agentic coding, computer use, and professional work at about one fifth of Astra's standard token price. GPT-6 Astra is still the model OpenAI called the most capable at the start of the month. It is no longer the only name on the page. Anyone writing a standard for the quarter should say which date they mean.

This article does not repeat benchmark percentages that were not opened on the primary post in this pass. If you need a specific Astra score, read OpenAI's post and system card and label the number as theirs. Do not invent a GPT-6.1 Astra. The September 29 announcement is GPT-6.1 Sol.

Most capable is not the default for every ticket

A flagship belongs on work where a miss is expensive and a person will review the result: a tangled owner dispute, a multi-document lease comparison, a coding change with tests. It is a waste on sorting mail. Sol and Luna exist so the flagship is not the model on every call.

Cybersecurity claims on a model card are not an invitation to point GPT-6 Astra at offensive work, and they are not a control for your own systems. Keep security testing inside the program your company already uses. Keep leasing and accounting on ordinary, reviewed workflows.

An OpenAI key still needs a model choice

innflow stores an OpenAI key under Settings, then BYOK. The key does not select GPT-6 Astra. If you want Astra on one node, set that ID and leave the high-volume nodes on a cheaper model. Check the ID after the September 29 releases so a workspace is not quietly aimed at last week's default.

The property management system remains the system of record. Astra can propose a reading of a file. It does not post the adjustment. Messages to residents, owners, and vendors wait for a person. That gate matters more on a model that sounds sure of itself.

Decide with a date on the page

Write "GPT-6 Astra, evaluated September 2026" in the runbook, plus the task it is allowed to draft. Revisit when you have a week of review notes next to GPT-6.1 Sol on the same task. Keep whichever needs less repair.

GPT-6 Astra is the early-September flagship. The later Sol models are how OpenAI priced capability downward. Use the flagship on purpose, not by leftover default.

Put the review on the workflow at innflow.

Ask whoever owns the OpenAI account which ID production used in the first week of September, and which ID it uses now. GPT-6 Astra may still be on a quiet workflow that nobody retargeted. Find those workflows before the next invoice explains them to you.

The useful question after September 29 is which workflows still name the September 3 flagship and which ones moved to a Sol model. Open the account usage export and group by model ID. Anything still on the early flagship needs an owner. Anything already moved needs the rubric from the old run, so you are not grading the new model with a feeling. innflow can hold that rubric on the canvas next to the step, but only after someone chooses the model on the node. A marketing page does not flip the node for you. Do not print benchmark percentages you have not re-read on the current announcement.

Write the model ID, the price you observed, and the pass rule in one note the on-call person can open.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Sol on September 29, 2026, near Astra on agent work, at about one fifth of Astra's standard token price. Grade one real job first.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What OpenAI shipped with GPT-6.1 Sol

GPT-6.1 Sol is OpenAI's September 29, 2026 addition to the GPT-6 line. The company describes it as an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol that comes close to GPT-6 Astra on agentic coding, computer use, and professional work, at about one fifth of Astra's standard input and output token prices. The announcement is here: Introducing GPT-6.1 Sol.

Developers call it in the API as gpt-6.1-sol. OpenAI lists standard prices of $2 per million input tokens, $0.10 per million cached input tokens, and $10 per million output tokens. The company says cached input is 95 percent below the standard input price and 50 percent below GPT-6 Sol's cached input price. That matters when an agent rereads the same lease file, vendor thread, or work order history across many turns.

GPT-6.1 Sol is available to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. OpenAI says it is not yet available in Chat. A faster serving option, GPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast, is planned for the coming days, with up to 8 times faster token generation than the standard speed in Codex. OpenAI's September 29 note points readers to this model. It does not announce a GPT-6.1 Astra.

On DeepSWE v1.1, OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol matches GPT-6 Astra at roughly one fifth of the cost, and beats GPT-6 Sol's best score by 6.4 points at a lower reasoning effort. Those are the lab's figures on its own evaluation, not an independent audit, and they are not a property-management score.

What the price change does and does not change

A lower token price does not make a model the system of record. Rent rolls, ledgers, and owner statements still live in the property management system. this Sol release can draft, compare, and propose. It should not post a charge, send a notice, or change a vendor assignment on its own.

The useful comparison is cost per finished task, not cost per million tokens in the abstract. A model that is cheaper per token can still be more expensive if it takes more turns, rereads a long file, or produces work a person has to redo. Cached input helps only when the same context is reused. A one-off question about a single invoice will not see that discount.

How a property team should try GPT-6.1 Sol

innflow can store an OpenAI key under Settings, then BYOK. Storing the key does not mean every new model ID is already selected on a live workflow. Open the model control on the node and confirm gpt-6.1-sol is the ID you intend before you point a daily process at it.

Pick one workflow that already has a clear finish line. Good candidates are a maintenance triage summary, a lease-clause comparison, or a vendor invoice check. Keep the acceptance criteria the same as the current process. Run this Sol release beside the model you use now. Count turns, review time, and the number of items a person sends back.

Outbound messages to residents, owners, and vendors stay with a person. The model can prepare the draft on a visual canvas, and a permission gate can hold the send until someone approves it. That split is the same whether the model is new this morning or a year old.

A short evaluation before you switch

Give the test a week of real tickets, not a single demo. Write down which cases got better, which stayed flat, and which still needed a manager. If the gain is only on clean examples, leave the live workflow where it is.

this Sol release is a pricing and capability update inside a family that already includes Sol, Luna, and Astra. Treat it as a candidate for scoped agent work. Keep the property system as the record, and keep a person on anything that leaves the building.

When you want that review step in the product, start with innflow and define the request, the expected output, and the person who approves the send.

Keep the pilot inside work you can grade. A lease comparison is gradable. A vague request to "clean up the portfolio" is not. Write the pass rule before the first call, and store the outputs next to the rule so the next model release has a baseline waiting.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Gemini 3.8 is a September family: Flash and Flash Cyber on September 2, plus later Live and text-to-speech posts, not one model ID. Test one scoped job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
Gemini 3.8 is a family, not a single SKU

The card says Gemini 3.8. Google did not ship one model under that name. On September 2, 2026, Google introduced Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber. The post is here: Introducing Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.8 Flash Cyber. The same Gemini models blog also carries later posts for a Live model and for text-to-speech. Treat the name as the September family.

Flash is described as the workhorse: better than Gemini 3.7 Flash on software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning, at the same introductory price of $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens. Google calls it the best reasoning and coding model it has shipped at the speed and cost of 3.7 Flash. That price is an introductory rate. Confirm the current number before you forecast a quarter.

Flash Cyber is a separate variant for cybersecurity. Google says it is offered to trusted defenders through the Fairwind program, for vulnerability detection and automated patching. This note is not a guide to that work. Property teams should not point a general operations workflow at a model that exists for defensive security programs. If you are not in that program, you are not the audience for that SKU.

Live and speech are different jobs

The Live post and the text-to-speech posts are about conversation and voice, not about reading a rent roll faster. A live model that can talk is a different product surface from a text model that drafts a notice. Mixing them in one workflow because they share a family name will produce the wrong failure mode: a voice system that sounds confident about a balance it should not state.

If you evaluate voice later, keep it on a non-binding intake path. A resident can leave a request. A person, or a reviewed workflow, confirms the commitment. The model does not promise a repair window or a credit.

Using Gemini inside a property workflow

innflow supports a Google Gemini key under Settings, then BYOK. The key is stored as an encrypted secret. Choosing Flash on a node is a separate step from saving the key, and Flash Cyber is not a general default. Use the text workhorse for document and coding drafts. Leave the cyber variant out of leasing, accounting, and maintenance queues.

The property management system remains the system of record. A canvas workflow can summarize an export, draft a reply, or check a spreadsheet. A permission gate holds anything that would be emailed or texted. Residents, owners, and vendors hear from a person.

What to test

Run Flash on one scoped job you already measure: categorizing inbound maintenance, or drafting owner updates from numbers you paste in. Compare it with the Gemini model you use now on edit time and missed facts. Ignore family-wide slogans. Score the specific ID.

Gemini 3.8 is a set of September releases. Pick the text model if you pick one. Keep voice and cyber variants in their own lanes, and keep a person on the send.

Start with innflow when you want that lane drawn on a canvas.

When a family shares a name, the runbook has to name the variant. "We use Gemini 3.8" is not an instruction. "We use Flash for draft classification, and we do not use Flash Cyber" is an instruction. Put that sentence where the on-call person can see it.

Flash Cyber is not a model for a leasing assistant. Google limits that variant to trusted defenders in the Fairwind program, for finding vulnerabilities and proposing patches. Name the program and stop. Ordinary classification and drafting, if you use this family at all, belong on Flash at the published introductory price, and only after you confirm the ID on the node. innflow can store a Google Gemini key. It does not enroll you in Fairwind, and it should not be described as if it does. Live and speech posts are separate products. Do not fold them into a text workflow because they share a family name.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Fireworks Research released Ember-1 on September 23, 2026, trained on Kimi K3 to answer with roughly 40 percent fewer tokens at similar quality. Test one job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What Fireworks Research shipped

Ember-1 is a specialized model from Fireworks Research, published on September 23, 2026. It is built on Kimi K3 and trained to cut reasoning tokens while keeping the answer. Fireworks says it delivers Kimi K3 quality with about 40 percent fewer tokens, and that the quality held on external benchmarks, live customer tests, and the company's own coding and agent work. The post is here: Introducing Ember-1.

The problem they describe is familiar to anyone running agents. Reasoning models can spend most of their tokens thinking rather than answering. In a multi-turn agent, earlier reasoning is sent back on every later turn, so the bill grows faster than the number of steps. Turning Kimi K3's effort setting down did not fix it, Fireworks says, because quality dropped. Ember-1 is their attempt to teach the model to skip reasoning that does not change the answer.

Fireworks says the training used its own data, not customer data, across math, coding, instruction following, conversation, search, tool use, and software engineering. Ember-1 is rolling out as a research preview on Fireworks serverless, beside the base Kimi K3 model. The company describes a two-week serverless window for research releases, with models kept if demand is there. It also offers training support so an enterprise can specialize Ember-1 further on its own data.

How to read the savings claim

The 40 percent figure is Fireworks' claim, measured on their workloads. A live A/B test they describe showed about 35 percent fewer tokens per task at comparable quality for two customers' coding traffic. One of those customers planned to expand Ember-1 after the test. That is vendor reporting. It is a reason to run your own comparison, not a promise for a leasing desk.

Token savings help when the task is repetitive and the answer is checkable. They help less when the model needs the long trace to avoid a bad recommendation. A shorter chain of thought on a vendor dispute can be a worse chain of thought. Measure the edit rate, not only the invoice from the model host.

Where Ember-1 sits for property operators

innflow does not have a native Fireworks key. Do not treat the Fireworks model as a switch inside the product. If your team already runs models through Fireworks, this preview is a candidate for high-volume classification and coding assistance. If you do not, there is nothing to turn on.

The operating rule does not change with the model. The property management system holds the balances and the lease. An agent on a visual canvas can propose a coding change or a summary. A person approves anything that would be sent to a resident, an owner, or a vendor. Permission gates are how that approval is enforced, whether the underlying model is the Fireworks model or something you already pay for.

A small pilot

If you have Fireworks access, pick one internal job with a known good answer: tagging maintenance requests, or drafting a script that reconciles a bank export. Run the Fireworks model next to Kimi K3 on the same set. Compare tokens, time, and how often a person rewrites the result. Keep resident-facing work out of the pilot.

the Fireworks model is a cost experiment from Fireworks Research, aimed at teams that already think in tokens. It is not a property product. Use it only where you can see the bill and the errors.

Reviewed workflows start at innflow.

Research previews also expire. Fireworks described a short serverless window. If a workflow depends on the Fireworks model, write down the date you will check whether the ID is still served. A model that disappears mid-month should fail closed, back to the model you already trust.

Fewer tokens is a vendor claim, measured on Fireworks tests. Repeat a small version on your text. Take a set of maintenance tickets the current model already handles, run them at the same quality bar, and compare token counts on the invoice, not in a screenshot of a benchmark table. If the count does not fall, keep the model you have. There is no Fireworks key in innflow. A research preview on their serverless tier is not a native node, and resident files should stay out of a preview you do not have a contract for. The underlying base is Kimi K3. That does not make the preview a Kimi product you already approved.
properties.Title: Ember-1 Trains a Model to Spend Fewer Tokens

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: DeepSeek released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on September 10, 2026: a 552 billion model with image input, called in the API as deepseek-flash. Test one scoped job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What DeepSeek released

On September 10, 2026, DeepSeek released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which it calls the smallest model in a new architecture family, with native visual understanding. The news post is Introducing DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. The API changelog for the same day is the operational source for what the API actually does: DeepSeek API changelog.

DeepSeek describes a 552 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model with a causal encoder-decoder design: about 8 billion parameters active on input and about 16 billion on output. It says the key-value cache needs about one quarter of the HBM and one eighth of the SSD of the previous generation, which is how it argues agent costs fall when cache hits dominate the bill. The API ID is deepseek-flash. Older names deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp route to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for compatibility. Those older flash models are retired.

The September 10 changelog also says DeepSeek will keep serving V4-Pro after September 14, 2026, with billing unchanged. A line on the news page described a plan to route V4-Pro calls to the new flash model. Follow the changelog: V4-Pro service continues. Do not tell a team that V4-Pro was shut off.

Scores, prices, and the peak window

DeepSeek's changelog lists its own results, including GPQA Diamond 90.9, Codeforces rating 3471, Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 90.6, DeepSWE v1.1 at 74.2, NL2Repo at 65.4, and Automation-Bench at 54.8. Cite them as DeepSeek's numbers.

The news post says API prices were reduced with this release, that peak and off-peak pricing continues, and that off-peak rates are half of peak rates, effective 04:00 UTC on September 10, 2026. The dollar table lives on DeepSeek's pricing page and is not repeated here. Read it for your account before you forecast. Flexible jobs, such as overnight classification, are the ones that can use the off-peak window. A coordinator waiting on a draft cannot.

A DeepSeek key is already a supported path

innflow supports a DeepSeek key under Settings, then BYOK. Saving it does not retarget workflows. If a node still says an older flash ID, know that those IDs currently route to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. That routing is a compatibility convenience. Set the ID you mean, which is deepseek-flash, so a later change does not surprise you.

Image understanding is new surface area. A photo of a maintenance issue can be summarized. The work order still gets created by the process you already trust, and the property management system remains the record. Residents, owners, and vendors still receive messages from a person.

Test the route you will actually call

Run ten text tasks and ten image tasks. Check amounts, unit numbers, and whether the model invented a cause. Compare cost at a peak hour and an off-peak hour so the price schedule is visible.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is a concrete API change with a named ID and a changelog you can point to. Use the changelog when the marketing page and the API disagree.

Hold the send on the canvas with innflow.

Image input is the feature most likely to be misused on day one. A photo can support a work order. It should not be the only record of damage, and it should not be uploaded if the lease or local rule limits what you collect. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash does not change that policy.

Read the changelog beside the news post. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is the new small model, and the changelog is the page that says older flash IDs route to it. The same changelog says the V4-Pro API continues, so do not turn off a Pro workflow because a news sentence sounded like a retirement. Pricing moved to a peak and off-peak split. Check Models and Pricing for the dollars, and try one image-backed work order only when your photo policy already allows the upload. Open-source support was promised. That is not the same sentence as a license you can quote today.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, 2026. It is faster than Sonnet 5, at the same token price, for scoped daily tasks. Test one job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What Anthropic shipped with Claude Sonnet 5.5

Claude Sonnet 5.5 is the second model in Anthropic's Claude 5.5 family, announced on September 28, 2026. The company positions it as a faster, lower-cost complement to Claude Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 is for complex work that needs careful judgment. Claude Sonnet 5.5 is aimed at well-scoped everyday tasks: fixing bugs, and producing documents, slides, and spreadsheets. Anthropic also says it has a sharp eye for design. The announcement is here: Introducing Claude Sonnet 5.5.

The list price matches Sonnet 5: $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, and $0.20 per million tokens for cache reads. Anthropic says the new model usually needs fewer tokens for the same work, and in its own testing it costs up to 30 percent less per task than Sonnet 5. It also generates output more than 30 percent faster, which Anthropic calls its fastest Sonnet so far.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, an agentic coding evaluation, Anthropic reports 70.6 percent for Claude Sonnet 5.5 against 10.3 percent for Sonnet 5. On GDPval-AA, a test of real-world work across occupations, it scores about two points below Opus 5.5. Anthropic is explicit that Opus 5.5 remains stronger at complex, open-ended work that needs sustained judgment. Those scores are the lab's, and they are not a leasing or maintenance benchmark.

Because its cybersecurity capability is comparable to Opus 5, this Sonnet release is the first Sonnet to launch with the cyber safeguards and fallbacks Anthropic uses on its most capable models. Biology safeguards match Sonnet 5. Anthropic says both target a narrow set of high-risk requests, and that routine software work and most life sciences work are unaffected. Claude Haiku 5.5, for high-volume and cost-sensitive applications, is planned for the coming weeks.

Where Claude Sonnet 5.5 fits in a stack

A property team does not need one model for every job. this Sonnet release is the candidate for work with a tight brief: a notice draft from an approved template, a spreadsheet of delinquent balances copied from the ledger, or a short code change in an internal tool. Opus-class models remain the candidate when the task is open-ended and a wrong turn is expensive.

Speed helps when a coordinator is iterating. It does not remove review. A faster draft of a late-rent notice is still a draft. The person who knows the lease and the local rule is the one who sends it.

How to try it without moving the books

innflow accepts an Anthropic key under Settings, then BYOK. Adding the key stores it as an encrypted workspace secret and shows only the last four characters. It does not automatically retarget every workflow to Claude Sonnet 5.5. Check the model ID on the node before a daily run uses it.

Keep the property management system as the system of record. The model can read an export or a summary you place in the workflow. It should not be the place balances are edited. On the canvas, put a permission gate in front of any step that would email a resident, an owner, or a vendor.

What to measure in the first week

Run the same ten tasks you already trust: five routine, five messy. Compare this Sonnet release with the model you use today on clarity, missed constraints, and minutes of human editing. If the win shows up only on the clean five, leave the messy work on the stronger model.

this Sonnet release is a daily-work model with a familiar price and a real speed claim from Anthropic. Use it where the task is scoped. Keep a person on the send, and keep the ledger where it already lives.

To put that gate on a workflow, get started with innflow.

Haiku 5.5 is not out yet. Do not design a three-model ladder that depends on a model Anthropic has only scheduled. Use the Sonnet you can call this week, and leave a note to revisit volume work when the smaller model has a price and an ID.
properties.Title: Claude Sonnet 5.5 for Everyday Agent Work

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Claude Mythos 5.1 launched September 1, 2026 as the same model as Fable 5.1, and Anthropic limits it to trusted access programs. Grade one real job first.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
Same model, narrower door

Anthropic released Claude Mythos 5.1 on September 1, 2026, together with Claude Fable 5.1. Anthropic's own words: they are the same model, with different safeguards. Fable 5.1 is generally available. Claude Mythos 5.1 is available only through trusted access programs. Its safeguards are aimed at cybersecurity and life sciences work. The announcement is Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1.

Two programs are named. The Cyber Verification Program provides access, for defensive security work, to certain Opus- and Sonnet-class models with reduced cyber safeguards. Anthropic says Mythos-class models are planned for that program later. The Life Sciences Verification Program is for life sciences professionals, with safeguards shaped for research and development, and other safeguards left in place. Anthropic says the first life sciences participants are enrolled with the US government, with broader access planned. Claude Security, Anthropic's product for scanning code and suggesting patches for a person to review, is also described as powered by Claude Mythos 5.1.

This is not a how-to for getting around those limits. Property operators are not the audience for a reduced-safeguard cyber model. If your company does defensive security research, you already know how vendor access programs work. Everyone else should stop at the name.

What Anthropic says changed since Mythos 5

Anthropic says Claude Mythos 5.1 is better aligned than Mythos 5 on most metrics it tracks. It reports a lower rate of reaching outside a test environment, less motivated reasoning, and a lower rate of ignoring explicit constraints. It also says testing still finds cases where the model can bypass approvals, and that long-context and multi-agent settings are less covered by its audits. Read that as a caution from the lab, not as a technique.

Because the underlying model matches Fable 5.1, the generally available way to use that capability for ordinary knowledge work is Fable, with Fable's safeguards. You do not need Claude Mythos 5.1 to draft an owner brief.

Do not plan a property workflow on it

innflow does not offer a Mythos switch, and it should not. There is no bring-your-own-key path that turns trusted access into a leasing bot. Teams that somehow have program access still do not point it at resident communication.

Daily work stays on models you can name in a contract: Sonnet, Opus, Fable, or whatever you have already reviewed. The property management system remains the system of record. A person sends every message to a resident, an owner, or a vendor. A permission gate is the product version of that rule.

The useful decision

Write Claude Mythos 5.1 down as restricted. Evaluate Claude Fable 5.1 if you need the capability class and you are allowed to buy it. Ignore any guide that offers a workaround. The restriction is the product decision.

For ordinary operations, the model on the card is a name to recognize, not a tool to deploy. Keep the work on a reviewed workflow.

That workflow can live in innflow.

If a vendor pitch offers Claude Mythos 5.1 as a general assistant for property managers, ask which access program they are in and what the safeguards still block. No program membership means they do not have the model. Do not build a workflow on a pitch.

Trusted access is a contracting problem before it is a technical one. Someone has to know whether the account is in a verification program, which queries are rerouted, and what the invoice does when a query is rerouted. Property operators should not build daily maintenance or leasing workflows on a model they cannot call. Keep defensive security work, if you have it, inside the program Anthropic named, and keep ordinary operations on a model you can select today. No blog post is a substitute for that membership. This note names the programs and stops there.

Write the model ID, the price you observed, and the pass rule in one note the on-call person can open.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Anthropic made Claude Fable 5.1 generally available on September 1, 2026 at $10 and $50 per million tokens, with much cheaper cache reads. Test one job.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders tracking model releases
properties.draft_blog:
What became generally available

On September 1, 2026, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1. They are the same model with different safeguards. Claude Fable 5.1 is the generally available one. It is offered to Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, on the Claude API as claude-fable-5-1, and through Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. The product page is Claude Fable. The joint announcement is Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1.

The price is $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Cache reads are $0.25 per million tokens, which Anthropic says is 75 percent less than Fable 5. The company estimates typical billed workloads cost about 25 percent less than Fable 5, and highly agentic workloads up to about 45 percent less, because so much of an agent run is rereading context. US-only inference is listed at 1.1 times the input and output price.

Anthropic describes Claude Fable 5.1 as a Mythos-level model for long-running coding and knowledge work: hours-long jobs, fewer easy shortcuts, fixes aimed at causes rather than symptoms. Cybersecurity and biology safeguards can route some requests to a less capable model. Anthropic says you are not charged Fable prices for those rerouted requests. Default use requires 30-day data retention for safety monitoring. Eligible enterprise customers can use a zero-data-retention arrangement until Enterprise Frontier Safeguards are in place. That enterprise option is rolling out in phases.

Expensive and general are still not unsupervised

Claude Fable 5.1 is the model you consider when a task spans many documents and a weaker model keeps dropping constraints. It is the wrong default for a two-line classification. At $50 per million output tokens, a sloppy prompt is a visible bill.

Safeguard routing is a product behavior, not a bug to route around. If a request comes back from a fallback model, read it as a fallback. Do not shop for a way to disable the safeguard. Property work rarely needs the restricted domains those safeguards target.

An Anthropic key, then a deliberate ID

innflow accepts an Anthropic key under Settings, then BYOK. The secret is encrypted. Choosing claude-fable-5-1 on a node is optional and should be rare. Most leasing and maintenance drafts belong on Sonnet-class models. Keep Fable for the hard, reviewed jobs.

The property management system remains the system of record. A long agent run can prepare a brief. A person decides what, if anything, is sent to a resident, an owner, or a vendor. Put that decision on a permission gate so a multi-hour run cannot finish by emailing someone.

Pilot one hard job

Choose a job you already escalate to a senior person: a messy owner packet, or a code change that touches billing. Compare Claude Fable 5.1 with your current strong model on corrections and on dollars, including cache reads. If the quality is flat, stay with the cheaper model.

Claude Fable 5.1 is the widely available Mythos-class release. Mythos 5.1 itself stays on trusted-access programs. Use the one you are allowed to use, on work that deserves the bill.

Gate the result with innflow.

Cache reads are where the discount lives. A workflow that sends a fresh copy of the same packet on every turn will not see the $0.25 rate. Structure the run so repeated context is actually cached, then read the invoice. Claude Fable 5.1 is only cheaper than Fable 5 if that pattern holds.

US-only inference at 1.1 times the price is a line item to notice if your account is not in the United States. Ask the owner of the Anthropic account which region the calls use before you forecast the bill. Rerouted requests, the ones safeguards send to a less capable model, are not billed at these rates. That is good for cost and confusing for quality, because a run can look cheap for the wrong reason. Log when a result was rerouted if the platform tells you. Then decide whether the task belongs on this model at all. Hours-long coding sessions still end in a human review before a change reaches a resident notice or a ledger.
