properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Set up an innflow VS Code integration so agent mode can list, inspect, and run deployed property workflows, with OAuth scopes and a human on the send step.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
The editor is already where the review happens

Most property teams that write any internal tooling already live in Visual Studio Code. Notice templates, small scripts, and the notes next to a workflow sit in one window. An innflow VS Code integration lets the agent in that window see the workflows themselves: names, deploy state, inputs, and logs.

innflow is property operations software with AI workflows on a visible canvas. It does not replace the property management system of record. VS Code does not become the system of record either. The integration gives the editor a scoped door into work that is already deployed.

This guide is the door. It covers the MCP file VS Code expects, the public API for jobs that are not an editor session, and a maintenance example where the useful first action is reading a failed log.

What VS Code adds, and what it should leave alone

VS Code, with GitHub Copilot in agent mode, can edit a workspace, run a terminal, and call MCP servers declared for that workspace or for the user. For a property engineer, that is a review bench. The diff is on screen. The checklist is a file. The agent can propose a change and wait.

The bench is blind to innflow until you connect it. Without the connection, people paste logs into chat and hope the summary matches the run. With an innflow VS Code integration, the agent can ask the workspace directly.

Keep the split clean. The editor owns files and review. innflow owns the deployed workflow, the credential, and the handoff a resident, owner, or vendor will eventually see. The agent can prepare. A person sends.

What the session is allowed to do

The hosted MCP endpoint is https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp. Sign-in is OAuth 2.1. You pick a workspace and approve scopes. There is no API key on this door, and the grant is revocable.

An authorized session can:

  • List workflows
  • Inspect one workflow
  • Execute a workflow only after it is deployed
  • Deploy a workflow, or return it to draft
  • List executions
  • Read execution details and the node log

Drafts do not execute. Read-only workspace members cannot call write endpoints. Those rules apply in the editor the same way they apply in a script.

The public API remains available for anything that should not depend on an open editor. Base URL: https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1. Create keys under Settings: API Keys. A key starts with inf_sk_ and is shown once. Docs and the OpenAPI document are linked from the API introduction.

Pass X-Innflow-Workspace when the work belongs to an organization workspace. Pass a fresh Idempotency-Key on create, import, duplicate, deploy, undeploy, and execute. The same key and the same body replay for 24 hours. The same key and a different body conflict.

Add the server in VS Code

Workspace MCP config lives in .vscode/mcp.json. That file can be committed. The OAuth grant cannot, and should not, be committed. The file only names the server.

{
  "servers": {
    "innflow": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp"
    }
  }
}

Reload the window, open Copilot agent mode, and ask it to list innflow tools. Complete the innflow sign-in, choose the workspace, and approve scopes. An unauthorized response before that approval is the server waiting, which is what you want on a fresh clone.

A user-level MCP config is fine for a person who works across many repos. A workspace file is better when the whole team should see the same server name in the property repo. Either way, the grant is personal.

Put a short rule in the repo instructions the agent already reads. Use the innflow server to list and inspect. Execute only a named deployed workflow. Do not send resident, owner, or vendor messages from the editor. If a prompt starts asking for an inf_sk_ key, stop and use the sign-in instead.

Worked example: a vendor dispatch that stopped

A maintenance coordinator queues after-hours calls through a deployed innflow workflow. Last night one run did not finish. The coordinator has a screenshot. The engineer has the repo, the dispatch notes, and VS Code.

The useful session is a read, then a decision.

  1. Ask the agent to list recent executions for the vendor-dispatch workflow.
  2. Ask it to open the failed execution and quote the node log, not a paraphrase of the screenshot.
  3. Compare the log to the checklist in the repo. Look for a missing input, a credential the workflow could not use, or a step that waited on a person and timed out.
  4. If the fix is a file, make the diff in VS Code and review it.
  5. If the fix is the canvas, change it in innflow. Deploy only after someone who owns maintenance agrees.
  6. Re-run with a new idempotency key only when the input is the same shape the workflow expects.

A first prompt that stays inside the line: "Using the innflow connection, list executions for the vendor dispatch workflow and show the latest failed node log. Do not deploy or execute." The second prompt happens after a person has read that log.

The agent will sometimes offer to text the vendor from the terminal. Decline. The workflow can hold a draft. The coordinator sends from innflow, on the credential the workspace already reviewed.

This is the daily shape of an innflow VS Code integration. The editor is the place the log gets read next to the notes. The canvas is the place the workflow changes state.

Scripts in the same repo

Some teams also keep a small runner in the repo: a script that executes one deployed workflow on a schedule. That runner should use a key, not the editor's OAuth session.

curl -X POST https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows/{workflowId}/execute \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: vendor-dispatch-replay-2026-09-29" \
  -d '{"input":{"ticketId":"WO-1842"}}'

Give the key an expiration that matches the trial or the season. Revoke it when the script is retired. Do not print the key in a VS Code task that commits its output. JSON errors include error, an optional code, and requestId. Keep X-Request-Id with the incident note.

Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor can share this API. The VS Code piece is the review bench, not a second operations product.

Controls and the outward MCP node

Scope the grant to the workspace that owns these workflows. Start with list and inspect. Execute a single named workflow. Deploy is a separate yes. Rotate access when roles change.

Unauthorized means sign-in is unfinished or the grant was removed. A write blocked for a read-only member means the role is correct. Execute blocked on a draft means the canvas was never deployed. An idempotency conflict means the key was reused with a different payload. Read the request id, then decide whether the retry is actually the same request.

innflow can also call out. Settings: MCP servers stores an external server, and an MCP node on the canvas can use its tools during a workflow. That outward path is for tools the workflow needs. The inward path is this integration: VS Code asking innflow what ran. Use the path that matches the question.

AES-256 covers data in transit and at rest. Customer data is not retained for model training. Private and VPC deployment stay available for teams that require them. The editor connection does not move that boundary.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. In this setup the proof you can check is local: a log that matches the canvas, a diff someone reviewed, and a send step that never left innflow.

How a maintenance week should feel

Monday is config. Commit .vscode/mcp.json with the URL and no secret. Each engineer signs in once. Ask agent mode for the workflow list and paste the names into the dispatch notes. Wrong workspace shows up here, while the only cost is a few minutes.

Tuesday is the last failed vendor run. The agent quotes the node log beside the checklist. The coordinator reads both. If the failure is a missing input, fix the source of that input. If the failure is a credential, fix it under the workspace credential, not by pasting a token into chat.

Wednesday is one replay of a ticket the coordinator chooses. New idempotency key. The engineer watches the execution appear on the canvas while the editor session reads the same log. Two screens, one run. That is the habit an innflow VS Code integration is supposed to build.

Thursday is a diff that does not deploy. Change a comment in the checklist, review it, and leave the canvas alone. The point is to practice stopping. Agent mode will offer to continue. The person closes the loop.

Friday is a five-line runbook in the repo: workflow name, who may execute, who texts the vendor, where a script key would live, and the request-id field to copy on failure. Next week's on-call person should be able to follow it without this article open.

If the team also keeps a scheduled runner, give that runner its own key and its own idempotency pattern. Do not reuse the editor grant. When the runner is retired, revoke the key the same day and say so in the notes.

A dispatch note the next shift can trust

The editor session ends. The next coordinator was not in it. Leave a note that stands alone: workflow name, execution id, unit or ticket id, the node that stopped or finished, and whether a vendor message is still unsent. Five fields. If the note is a paragraph of advice, rewrite it into the five fields.

Store the note where the shift already looks, and keep the same ids on the canvas. VS Code helped read the log. It is not the log. When someone challenges the note, you open the execution, not the chat. That habit is the difference between an innflow VS Code integration and a long transcript nobody will reopen.

If the next shift must replay the run, they use a new idempotency key and the input copied from the failed execution, corrected where the log showed a gap. They do not ask the agent to "try again" against a half-remembered ticket. The key, the input, and the person who texts the vendor are all named before the call goes out.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does an innflow VS Code integration replace the property management system?

No. Units, leases, and ledgers stay in the property management system. innflow runs the workflows around that system. VS Code is where people review files and logs.

Can the agent execute a draft workflow?

No. Deploy on the canvas first. Both the MCP session and the API refuse a draft. That gate is what keeps an experiment in the editor off a live dispatch.

Should the API key live in .vscode?

No. .vscode/mcp.json should contain the server URL only. Interactive work uses OAuth. A key belongs in the secret store for a script, and it is revoked if it lands in git.

Can Copilot message vendors from the terminal?

Do not allow that. The workflow may prepare the update. The person who owns the vendor relationship sends it from innflow.

What if two people retry the same dispatch?

Use one idempotency key for one real request. A retry of that same body replays the saved response for 24 hours. A different body needs a new key.

Put the log next to the notes

Connect the workspace. Ask for one failed execution. Read the node log beside the checklist you already keep in the repo. That is a working innflow VS Code integration: the editor for review, the canvas for the run, and a person on anything a vendor will receive.

Get started at app.innflow.ai/signup or open an existing workspace at app.innflow.ai.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: See how an innflow Quinn integration runs on the workflow canvas, shares deployed workflows with other agents, and keeps a person on every real send step.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
Quinn already sits in the workspace

Quinn is the innflow agent people meet inside the product. In the workspace, Quinn can gather context, propose a next step, and hand that step to a person. A scheduling note is the clearest picture: Quinn offers a few times that work for both sides, and a teammate confirms before anything is booked. An innflow Quinn integration is how that agent stays tied to a deployed workflow, a credential, and a visible handoff.

The other harness guides in this series are about external clients calling in: Codex, VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Muse Code, and Devin. Quinn is the inside path. Same canvas. Same rule that a resident, owner, or vendor message waits for a person. Different door.

innflow is property operations software with AI workflows. Quinn is an agent on that system, not a replacement for the property management system of record.

What Quinn is for

Property work fails in the gap between a request and the next responsible person. Someone asks for a call. Someone needs a packet prepared. Someone is waiting on a vendor window. Quinn is useful when the next step can be prepared from context the workspace already has: calendars the workflow can see, a checklist, a prior execution.

Quinn is not a side inbox. If Quinn proposes three times, the times are a draft until a person accepts them. If Quinn prepares a notice, the notice stays a draft until the owner of that relationship sends it. That is the product behavior to protect while you connect more tools around Quinn.

The canvas is the integration surface. You can see the flow, the status, and where a human handoff sits. A chat transcript alone is not the operational record. The execution is.

The same doors the other agents use

Quinn runs inside innflow, so it does not need a separate MCP login to see its own workspace. The workflows it should call are the workflows you deploy on the canvas. Skills, under Settings: Skills, give Copilot and AI Agent nodes reusable instructions. A skill has a name, a description, instructions, and a side-effect level. Skills add context. They do not grant new permissions, and you cannot delete a skill that active workflows still use.

When Quinn's workflow needs a tool from outside, register that tool as an MCP server under Settings: MCP servers. The MCP node on the canvas can call a specific tool directly, or an AI Agent node can choose among the tools you connected. The server URL is yours to confirm. Authentication stays on that server's terms, stored encrypted at rest when you provide a key.

External harnesses reach the same workflows through the hosted MCP endpoint https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp with OAuth 2.1, or through the public API at https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1. A Codex session and Quinn are not two sources of truth. They are two clients of one deployed workflow. If both can execute it, give each run its own idempotency key so a helpful overlap does not double the work.

API keys, for the external path, are created in Settings: API Keys. They start with inf_sk_ and are shown once. Read-only members cannot write. Draft workflows cannot execute. Those rules apply to Quinn's workflow and to every harness that calls it.

Build the workflow Quinn should run

Start with one job Quinn already resembles: proposing times and handing them to a person.

  1. On the canvas, build a workflow that reads the context it is allowed to read and produces a short list of options.
  2. End the autonomous part at a handoff. The handoff is a person, named by role, who confirms or rejects.
  3. Attach a skill if the instructions are stable: tone, what to include, what to leave out. Keep the side-effect level honest.
  4. If a calendar or another system is required, connect it with the credential that belongs to the operation, or with an MCP server you have reviewed.
  5. Deploy the workflow. Until you deploy, neither Quinn nor an external client can execute it.
  6. Run it once with a test that your team can recognize as a test. Read the node log.

A prompt you might give Quinn inside the product: "Propose three times for a call with Dominic and me. Do not book the meeting. Hand the times to me." The workflow should make that last sentence structural, not polite. The handoff node is the control. The sentence in chat is the reminder.

This is the core of an innflow Quinn integration. The agent is allowed to prepare. The workflow is allowed to run because it was deployed. The book, the send, and the vendor call wait.

Worked example: the call, then the packet

A prospect asks for time with a leasing lead. Quinn can see the windows the connected calendar exposes and the lead's constraints the workflow already encodes. Quinn returns three times. The lead picks one. Only then does a second step book, and only on the credential leasing trusts.

Later the same prospect becomes an applicant. The packet workflow is a different deployed workflow. Quinn can start it only when the lead says the application is real. An external harness, Cursor or Claude Code, might inspect that same packet workflow while an engineer updates a checklist in a repo. Both clients must tolerate the same gates:

  • Inspect is cheap and should be the first call.
  • Execute names one workflow and one input.
  • The idempotency key includes the person and the attempt.
  • The applicant-facing message is sent from innflow by leasing.

If Cursor executes the packet and Quinn also executes it, you want one of those calls to replay. That happens when they share an idempotency key and an identical body. It does not happen when each client invents a key. Agree the key in the runbook. A workable pattern is the applicant id plus the workflow slug plus the calendar day.

Deploy stays rare. Quinn proposing times does not imply Quinn publishing a new workflow version. The person who owns the canvas deploys. Everyone else calls what is already live.

Credentials, BYOK, and instructions

Provider keys for model access, if your plan uses them, live under Settings: BYOK. innflow can store keys for providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, and others. The settings page shows that a key exists and its last four characters. Removing a key returns nodes to the platform behavior on your plan. Quinn does not need a copied key in a prompt.

Skills are the instruction layer. Write them as if a new coordinator will read them next month. Name the inputs. Name the handoff. Name the messages Quinn must not send. A skill shared with the organization updates on the next execution. A personal skill stays with the person. Pick on purpose.

External MCP tools are the action layer. Before Quinn's agent node can choose a tool, someone has confirmed the server URL, the credential, and the operations that server exposes. Tool discovery is not approval of every possible call. Direct execution mode, where the workflow selects one tool and one input, is the tighter pattern for a resident-facing flow. Agentic choice fits when a person still sits on the handoff after the tool returns.

Encryption is AES-256 in transit and at rest. Customer data is not retained for model training. Private and VPC deployment remain available. Quinn uses that boundary. Connecting another harness does not move it.

How Quinn relates to the external harnesses

Use Quinn when the person is already in innflow and the job is operational: propose, prepare, hand off. Use Codex, VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Muse Code, or Devin when the person is in a repository and the job is the files plus a call into a deployed workflow. The innflow Quinn integration and those harness integrations should name the same workflow ids. If the names drift, you have two processes.

A practical weekly check:

  • List the workflows Quinn is allowed to start. Each one is deployed.
  • List the workflows each external harness is allowed to execute. The list is short.
  • Read one execution from each path. The logs should look like the canvas.
  • Confirm the send step is still a person.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. For Quinn, the proof is the handoff you can point at: three times proposed, one person confirming, nothing booked before that confirm.

A coordinator's first week with Quinn

Monday, pick the scheduling workflow and no other. Deploy it with a handoff at the end. Ask Quinn for three times on a test that your own team will see. Confirm that nothing books before a person taps one time. If a booking happens early, the handoff is in the wrong place. Fix the canvas before any prospect is involved.

Tuesday, write the skill. Short instructions: which calendar, how many options, the sentence Quinn uses, and the line that says a person confirms. Share it with the organization only after two people have used it. A personal skill is enough for the trial.

Wednesday, connect one external tool if the workflow truly needs it. Register the MCP server, call one tool in direct mode, and read the node log. Agentic choice can wait. Direct mode is easier to explain to a new coordinator, which is the standard for an innflow Quinn integration.

Thursday, invite one external harness to inspect the same workflow. Not to redesign it. The engineer in Cursor or Claude Code should see the same inputs the coordinator sees. If the lists differ, you have two workflows or two workspaces. Stop and reconcile the ids.

Friday, agree the idempotency pattern for any execute that both Quinn and a harness might start. One line in the runbook is enough. Then run a single test applicant, read the log, and send nothing to a real resident. The week is successful when a new teammate can point at the handoff and say who confirms.

Leave BYOK and extra provider keys alone unless a specific node requires them. Quinn does not get better because a key was pasted into a prompt. The skill, the handoff, and the deployed workflow are the parts that change the work.

What a new coordinator is shown

Show the canvas, not a tour of every harness. Open the scheduling workflow. Point at the step where Quinn proposes times. Point at the handoff. Click a past execution and read the log together. Then show the single line in the runbook that says who confirms. A new coordinator who can find those three things can work the innflow Quinn integration without a second briefing.

Mention the external harnesses only as clients of the same workflow. They are how an engineer inspects inputs while fixing a checklist. They are not a second Quinn. If the coordinator never opens Cursor, nothing about their day should change. The handoff stays theirs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does an innflow Quinn integration replace our property management system?

No. The property management system remains the system of record. Quinn and the workflows around Quinn operate on top of that record.

Can Quinn execute a workflow that is still a draft?

No. Deploy the workflow first. Drafts do not run, for Quinn or for any external client.

Can Quinn email a resident or book a meeting alone?

Design the workflow so the send and the booking sit after a human handoff. Quinn can propose times and prepare a draft. The person confirms.

Do we need a separate API key for Quinn?

Quinn works inside the workspace. API keys are for external scripts and harnesses calling https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1. Hosted MCP clients use OAuth at https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp.

What if Quinn and Cursor both start the same packet?

Share an idempotency key and an identical request body so the second call replays the first for 24 hours. Different bodies require different keys and a person to notice.

Propose, hand off, then send

Put Quinn on one deployed workflow with a visible handoff. Let a person confirm the times, the packet, or the vendor step. Let external harnesses call that same workflow only when they can name it and read the log. That is an innflow Quinn integration a property team can explain to a new coordinator in a single sitting.

Get started at app.innflow.ai/signup or open the workspace at app.innflow.ai.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Configure an innflow Muse Code integration in settings.json so the agent can run deployed property workflows after OAuth, with a person on the send step.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
A long session still needs a deployed workflow

Muse Code is Meta's terminal coding agent. You run it in a project, it plans a change across the repo, and it can keep working longer than a single edit. Property teams feel that length during owner-reporting week: templates, checklists, and a workflow that already knows how the pack is assembled. An innflow Muse Code integration lets that session call the workflow instead of re-describing it in chat.

innflow is property operations software with AI workflows on a visible canvas. The property management system stays the system of record. Muse Code stays the harness in the terminal. The connection is OAuth into a workspace, then list, inspect, and, when a person agrees, execute.

This guide is about Muse Code the coding agent. It covers the settings file, a quarterly owner-pack example, and the public API for runs that should not sit inside an interactive session.

What Muse Code is good at here

Muse Code plans, edits, and checks work in a repository, with approvals and an event log for the session itself. A property repo might hold the owner letter, the checklist of figures the workflow expects, and a note about which workflow id is deployed. Muse Code can hold that context for a long task.

The operational record is still the innflow execution. If the session only talks about the pack, you have a story. If it reads the log, you have the run. The innflow Muse Code integration is how the session gets from story to log.

Set the server as optional if you want Muse Code to keep working when innflow is unreachable. A required server aborts the run when the connection fails. Optional is the kinder default for a reporting week.

What the signed-in agent can call

The endpoint is https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp. The hosted innflow MCP server uses OAuth 2.1. You approve a workspace and a set of scopes. The grant can be revoked. You do not paste an API key into the settings file for this door.

An authorized Muse Code session can:

  • List workflows
  • Inspect a workflow
  • Execute a workflow that has been deployed
  • Deploy, or return a workflow to draft
  • List executions
  • Read execution details and node logs

Draft workflows do not execute. Read-only members do not get write endpoints. Approvals inside Muse Code are a second belt. They do not replace the workspace role.

The public API is https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1. Create keys in Settings: API Keys. Each key starts with inf_sk_ and is displayed once. Details sit in the API introduction.

Send X-Innflow-Workspace for an organization workspace. Send Idempotency-Key on create, import, duplicate, deploy, undeploy, and execute. Identical retries replay for 24 hours. A mismatched body conflicts.

Settings file for Muse Code

User settings live at ~/.config/muse/settings.json. The file must include schema_version set to 1. A missing file is fine, because Muse Code has defaults. A file you create without the schema version fails at startup.

Declare the server under mcpServers. Current Muse Code builds use that key with transport set to streamable_http:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "mcpServers": {
    "innflow": {
      "transport": "streamable_http",
      "url": "https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp",
      "mode": "optional"
    }
  }
}

Merge this into the file you already have. Do not keep a second block under a different key name beside mcpServers. Muse Code will refuse the config. If an older file used another key, move those servers into mcpServers and delete the duplicate.

Start a new session. Ask Muse Code to list innflow tools. Complete the OAuth sign-in it prints. The command is often muse mcp login innflow, and the exact line on your build is the one to run. Tokens refresh after that. muse mcp logout innflow drops the grant. Run /mcp in the session to see the live inventory.

Leave headers empty for this server. OAuth is the authentication. A bearer token in a shared settings file is a leaked key.

In the project's AGENTS.md, tell Muse Code to inspect before execute, to name the workflow, and to leave owner and resident messages inside innflow.

Worked example: the quarterly owner pack

A portfolio manager wants the same pack every quarter: a checklist, a drafted narrative, and a workflow that gathers the operational items the canvas already knows how to collect. The letter template is in the repo. The workflow is deployed.

  1. Ask Muse Code to list workflows and identify the owner-pack workflow.
  2. Inspect its inputs. Compare them to the checklist file. Stop on any mismatch.
  3. Let Muse Code edit the narrative template. You review the diff.
  4. When the inputs match, execute once, with a new idempotency key that includes the property and the quarter.
  5. Read the execution log inside the same session. The pack is not done because the narrative sounds finished. It is done when the log says the nodes finished.
  6. The manager sends the owner update from innflow.

Prompt the first step without a verb that changes state: "Using the innflow connection, inspect the owner pack workflow and list inputs. Do not execute." That sentence is the working pattern for an innflow Muse Code integration.

Muse Code can run for a long time and fan work out. Length is not permission to deploy. If the canvas needs a change, the person who owns reporting deploys it after they have looked at the flow. The session can prepare the checklist. It should not undeploy production because a branch of the task looked stuck.

Headless runs and the API

A quarterly job that starts from CI is a script, not a conversation. Use a key with an expiration that covers the close, then revoke it.

curl -X POST https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows/{workflowId}/execute \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: owner-pack-2026-q3-property-14" \
  -d '{"input":{"propertyId":"14","quarter":"2026-Q3"}}'

Muse Code can help you write the script in the repo. The key stays in the CI secret store. Failures include error, an optional code, and requestId. Keep X-Request-Id on the incident.

Interactive sessions stay on MCP. The job stays on the API. That split is what keeps a reporting experiment from borrowing a production key.

Failures and the canvas calling out

Unauthorized means login is not finished. Run the login command Muse Code printed, then start a new session if the inventory is stale. A read-only failure means the role cannot deploy or execute. A draft failure means the workflow was never deployed. An idempotency conflict means this body is not the body that key already saved.

innflow can call other MCP servers from the canvas. Register them under Settings: MCP servers and use an MCP node. That outward call is the workflow using a tool. The Muse Code connection is the engineer using the workflow. Put both in the runbook so a long session does not get debugged as the wrong one.

AES-256 covers transit and storage. Customer data is not retained for model training. Private and VPC deployment remain available. A settings.json entry does not widen access past the scopes you approved.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. For the owner pack, the check is concrete: one execution log, one reviewed narrative, one send that happened in innflow.

Approvals while the session is still going

Muse Code can stay with a task longer than a quick edit. Length needs checkpoints, or the owner pack grows a narrative that nobody compared to the log. Set three checkpoints in the prompt: after inspect, after the template diff, and after execute. Do not let the session cross a checkpoint without a person.

Use mode optional on the innflow server so a network blip does not abort the writing task. The writing can continue. The execute cannot. If /mcp does not show innflow, stop the operational half and fix login. Do not invent the log from memory while the server is down.

For the quarter, keep a close note in the repo: property id, workflow id, idempotency key pattern, and the manager who sends. Muse Code should read that note at the start of every session. An innflow Muse Code integration without the note depends on whatever the model remembers from yesterday.

Run one property end to end before you fan the work out. Parallel work is attractive during close. It is also how two sessions execute the same pack with two keys. Single-thread the first property. When the log, the narrative, and the send all match, then decide whether a second property can run beside it.

After close, log out the MCP grant on machines that were borrowed for the week. Leave the settings.json URL in place if the team will do this again. Remove any CI key that existed only for the quarter. The next close should start from a fresh key and the same workflow id, not from a secret someone still has in a laptop.

If the narrative and the log disagree, the log wins. Edit the letter. Do not edit the execution to match the prose.

The letter may use only what the log returned

Owner letters pick up numbers from somewhere. For this workflow, the somewhere is the execution, not a guess in the prompt. Before Muse Code drafts a sentence that states a count, a date, or a status, it should point at the node output that contains it. If the output is missing, the sentence waits. The letter can say the item is not in this run. It should not fill the blank.

Keep a field list in the repo: the outputs the pack workflow promises. When the canvas changes those outputs, change the list in the same week. Muse Code reads the list at the start of the session. A sentence that cites a field outside the list gets deleted in review, even if it sounds plausible.

This rule is what makes an innflow Muse Code integration safe for a portfolio audience. The agent can write clearly. It can arrange the checklist. It cannot become a second ledger. The property management system and the execution log remain the places a figure is allowed to come from. The manager who sends the letter is the person who accepts that the figures match.

If a stakeholder asks for a figure the workflow does not produce, add the field on the canvas, deploy it with a witness, and run one property again. Do not ask the session to estimate. Estimation is how a quarterly pack becomes a dispute.

Save the field list next to the letter template and review both when the quarter opens, not when the letter is due. If a promised output disappeared from the latest execution, take it out of the letter before drafting begins. Muse Code can help you find the missing name. It should not help you replace the missing name with a nearby figure from an older pack.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does an innflow Muse Code integration replace the property management system?

No. Ledgers, leases, and units stay in the property management system. innflow runs the pack workflow. Muse Code is the terminal client.

Can Muse Code execute a draft?

No. Deploy the workflow on the canvas first. Execute is refused until that is true.

Should the settings file contain an API key?

Not for hosted innflow MCP. Use OAuth. Create an inf_sk_ key only for a script or CI job, and store it outside settings.json.

Can the session send the owner letter?

Leave the send in innflow. The session can prepare the narrative and start the deployed workflow. The manager sends.

What if the quarterly job runs twice?

Use an idempotency key that names the property and the quarter. The second identical request replays the first response for 24 hours.

One pack, one log, one sender

Add the server. Sign in. Inspect the owner-pack workflow. Execute once. Read the log before anyone calls the quarter done. That is an innflow Muse Code integration a portfolio team can repeat.

Get started at app.innflow.ai/signup or open the workspace at app.innflow.ai.
properties.Title: innflow Muse Code Integration for Property Teams

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Set up an innflow Devin integration over HTTP MCP so a long session can inspect logs and run deployed property workflows, with a person on the send step.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
A long session is still a client

Devin, from Cognition, is built for work that outlasts a single prompt. It can keep a session open, read a repository, and come back with a proposed change. Property operations have tasks like that: a move-out workflow that stalled overnight, a log nobody read until morning, a fix that should be a note before it is a deploy. An innflow Devin integration gives that session a scoped view of the workflows and the executions.

innflow remains the place the workflow actually runs. The canvas is visible. Handoffs are explicit. The property management system remains the system of record. Devin does not become a second property system because it was patient.

This guide covers the custom MCP setup for Devin, a move-out example that is mostly reading, and the API path for a trigger that should not wait on a session.

Where Devin fits a property team

Some work is a diff. Some work is a watch. Move-out sits in between. The repo may hold the checklist and the resident-letter template. The live steps sit on an innflow workflow: inspection, deposit items, vendor, handoff to a person. When a run sticks, the useful artifact is the node log plus a proposed change, not an unsupervised retry loop.

Devin can hold that investigation across a longer session than a person wants to babysit. The innflow Devin integration is what makes the investigation about the real run. Without it, the session is guessing from whatever someone pasted at the start.

Constrain the session in the prompt and in the product. Read logs freely. Execute only a named deployed workflow. Deploy only after a person has seen the canvas. Never message the resident from the session.

What the connection can do

Use the hosted endpoint https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp with HTTP, the streamable HTTP transport. Sign-in is OAuth 2.1. Choose the workspace and approve scopes. Revoke the grant when the investigation is over or the operator changes.

The session can:

  • List workflows
  • Inspect one workflow
  • Execute a deployed workflow
  • Deploy a workflow or undeploy it back to draft
  • List executions
  • Read execution details and node logs

Drafts will not execute. Read-only workspace members cannot write. A long session does not earn an exception by waiting.

Triggers that are just triggers should use the public API: https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1. Keys from Settings: API Keys start with inf_sk_ and are shown once. The API introduction is the reference for workspaces, idempotency, and error ids.

X-Innflow-Workspace picks an organization. Idempotency-Key protects create, import, duplicate, deploy, undeploy, and execute. Same key, same body, replay for 24 hours. Same key, new body, conflict.

Add a custom MCP server in Devin

Organization admins can add a server that is not in a marketplace. In Devin, open Customize, then MCPs, then Add custom MCP. Name it innflow. Choose the HTTP transport. Set the server URL to https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp. Save, then use the test or sign-in step the product shows for HTTP servers. Complete innflow OAuth, pick the workspace, and approve scopes.

On the Devin CLI, the same idea is a URL add:

devin mcp add innflow https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp

A URL is treated as HTTP. Keep the config's local or user scope if the grant should not be shared through git. Project scope is appropriate only for the server name and URL, never for a token.

Do not put an inf_sk_ key in the MCP headers for this hosted server. OAuth is the door. A key in a Devin org config is a key every session might see.

Tell the session, in the playbook or the prompt, to start with list and inspect, to quote node logs, and to stop before deploy and before any resident message. The prompt is guidance. The workspace role is the control.

Worked example: the move-out that stalled

A move-out workflow is deployed. One execution from last night is still incomplete. The resident coordinator needs to know which node stopped. The engineer would rather read that answer than reconstruct it from memory.

  1. Ask Devin to list executions for the move-out workflow and identify the incomplete one.
  2. Ask it to quote the last node log and the input that run received.
  3. Compare the input to the checklist in the repo. A missing deposit flag is a data problem. A node waiting on approval is a person problem.
  4. If the fix is a template, Devin can edit the repo. Review the diff in the morning with the person who owns move-outs.
  5. If the fix is the canvas, change it in innflow and deploy as a separate, witnessed step.
  6. Do not re-execute against the resident until that person says the packet is safe to repeat. Use a new idempotency key when you do.
  7. Any resident update is sent from innflow.

The overnight prompt should be boring on purpose: "Using the innflow connection, read the latest incomplete move-out execution and quote the node log. Do not deploy, undeploy, execute, or message anyone." That is the innflow Devin integration at its best. The session spends time. It does not spend authority.

In the morning the coordinator reads the quoted log on the canvas and confirms it matches. Then someone decides. The decision is not "Devin was confident." The decision is the log plus the checklist.

A plain trigger, when you do not need a session

If the only need is to start a deployed workflow from a system you already run, skip the agent. Call the API with a key stored in that system.

curl -X POST https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows/{workflowId}/execute \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: move-out-2026-09-29-unit-4b" \
  -d '{"input":{"unitId":"4B"}}'

Devin can draft this call while investigating. It should read the key from an environment variable in the example and leave a placeholder in the repo. On errors, save requestId and X-Request-Id next to the unit id.

Expire keys. Revoke them when the investigation ends if the key was created just for it. A long-lived key for a long-lived session is how access outlives the project.

Failure meanings, and innflow calling out

Unauthorized: OAuth is incomplete or the grant was revoked. Read-only: the member cannot write, so do not escalate the role to finish an investigation. Draft: deploy on the canvas before execute. Idempotency conflict: this request is not the saved one. Read it. A long session that retries through a conflict will create noise, not clarity.

Separately, a workflow can call an external MCP server. That configuration lives under Settings: MCP servers and an MCP node on the canvas. It is the outward door. Devin's custom server is the inward door. Document them as different names so an overnight note does not send the morning person to the wrong screen.

AES-256 encryption applies in transit and at rest. Customer data is not retained for model training. Private and VPC deployment stay available for teams that need them. A Devin session inherits the scopes you approved and nothing broader.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. The proof that matters on a stalled move-out is the node log quoted accurately, and a resident message that waited for a person.

The morning review of an overnight note

An overnight Devin session should leave a note a coordinator can read in five minutes. The note has four parts: the execution id, the quoted node log, the input that run received, and a proposed next step that does not include sending a message. If any part is missing, the session is not done, even if the prose is long.

The coordinator opens the same execution on the canvas and checks the quote. A mismatch means the session summarized instead of quoting. Go back to the log. Do not act on the paraphrase. This comparison is the point of an innflow Devin integration. The session can watch. The canvas still judges.

Only after the quote matches do you talk about a fix. A template fix is a diff in the repo, reviewed like any other change. A canvas fix is a deploy, done by the person who owns move-outs, with a fresh look at the flow. The overnight session does not get to unfold that deploy because it was left running.

If a retry is truly required, the coordinator chooses the unit and the idempotency key. Devin can prepare the request. The person sends it. One unit. Then read the new log before a second unit is even discussed.

Close the loop in the playbook. What Devin may do unattended: list, inspect, quote logs, draft a repo diff. What waits for morning: deploy, undeploy, execute, anything a resident could receive. Write those two lists where the next investigation will see them. A long-running harness will fill any permission you leave unnamed.

When the investigation ends, remove org-level access that was added only for it, or narrow the scopes back to the people who operate move-outs every week. A custom MCP server pointed at production is not a souvenir.

Write the playbook before the first overnight run

Do not discover the boundaries at 1 a.m. Write them while everyone is awake. The playbook names the move-out workflow id, the workspace, and the sentence Devin must use to quote logs: the execution id, then the node text, with no paraphrase ahead of the quote. It names the morning owner. It names the channel where the note appears, which should be a place the coordinator already checks.

The playbook also lists forbidden tools in plain language. No resident message. No owner message. No vendor message. No deploy. No undeploy. Execute only if the morning owner has replied with the unit id and the idempotency key. A playbook that says "use judgment" will be interpreted as permission. A playbook that lists verbs is something you can audit.

Run the playbook once during the day, with a test unit, while the coordinator watches the canvas. Confirm the note matches the log. Then, and only then, allow an overnight investigation. The first real night should still be read-only. Add execute on a later night if the quotes have been accurate all week. That ladder is the innflow Devin integration a team can defend.

Keep one sample note from a day-time test in the playbook, with the execution id redacted if you must, so the next overnight run has a shape to copy. The sample shows the quote first and the suggestion second. Sessions that invert that order get sent back. The coordinator should be able to compare a new note to the sample in a minute and decide whether it is ready for a human decision.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does an innflow Devin integration replace the property management system?

No. The property management system remains the system of record. innflow runs the move-out workflow. Devin is a client that can read logs and call deployed workflows inside the scopes you approved.

Can a long session execute a draft because it prepared a fix?

No. Execute requires a deployed workflow. Preparation in the repo does not deploy the canvas.

Should Devin store an innflow API key?

Not for the hosted MCP connection. Use OAuth. Use an inf_sk_ key only for a non-interactive trigger, stored in that system's secret manager.

Can Devin text the resident about the move-out?

No. Keep that send in innflow. The session can quote the log and prepare a template. The coordinator sends.

How do we keep a retry from doubling the move-out run?

Put the unit and the date, or the attempt, in the idempotency key. Reuse the key only when the request body is identical.

Let the session read. Let a person ship.

Add the HTTP server. Sign in. Point Devin at one stalled execution. Quote the log. Decide in the morning, on the canvas, with the coordinator. That is a responsible innflow Devin integration.

Start at app.innflow.ai/signup or open app.innflow.ai.
properties.Title: innflow Devin Integration for Property Workflows

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Add an innflow Cursor integration in mcp.json so agent mode can inspect and run deployed property workflows, with OAuth scopes and a person still on send.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
Agent mode in the editor needs a workflow it can name

Cursor is where a lot of property engineers now review a change: a template, a script, a checklist, a small internal tool. Agent mode can edit that project and call MCP servers configured for it. An innflow Cursor integration is the missing name. The agent can list the workflows in a workspace, inspect the one you mean, and run it only after it is deployed.

innflow is the operations layer: AI workflows on a visible canvas, with handoffs and permissions you can see. The property management system stays the system of record. Cursor stays the editor. Neither one has to pretend to be the other.

This guide shows the project config, the sign-in, a leasing example, and the API path for anything that should run without the editor open.

What you want Cursor to touch

A leasing change often starts as a sentence. "The applicant packet needs the pet addendum field." That sentence becomes a checklist edit, sometimes a workflow edit, and always a question about what production currently expects. Cursor is a good place to hold the sentence next to the files.

It is a bad place to invent the production state. The deployed workflow is the production state. An innflow Cursor integration lets the agent read it. The person still decides whether today's diff is allowed to deploy.

Keep messages to applicants out of agent mode. The workflow can prepare them. The leasing owner sends them from innflow.

The actions behind the connection

Point Cursor at https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp. Authentication is OAuth 2.1. You select a workspace and approve scopes. The grant is revocable and it is not an API key.

After approval the agent can:

  • List workflows
  • Inspect one workflow
  • Execute a deployed workflow
  • Deploy a workflow or return it to draft
  • List executions
  • Read execution details and node logs

A draft will not run. A read-only member will not get write calls. If agent mode insists, the platform is correct and the prompt is wrong.

For a runner outside the editor, use https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1 with a key from Settings: API Keys. Keys start with inf_sk_ and are shown once. The API introduction documents workspaces, idempotency, and errors.

X-Innflow-Workspace selects an organization workspace. Idempotency-Key makes create, import, duplicate, deploy, undeploy, and execute safe to retry when the body is unchanged. A different body with the same key conflicts on purpose.

Project config that can be committed

Create .cursor/mcp.json in the repo:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "innflow": {
      "url": "https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp"
    }
  }
}

If the editor asks for a transport, choose HTTP, the streamable HTTP form. Save the file. Open agent mode and ask it to list innflow tools. Finish sign-in in the browser, pick the workspace, and approve scopes.

Commit the JSON. Do not commit a token, a bearer header, or an inf_sk_ value. The URL is not a secret. The grant is.

A global Cursor MCP entry is fine for one person hopping repos. The project file is better when a teammate should see the same server name on a fresh clone. They still sign in as themselves.

Add a few lines where Cursor already reads project rules. List and inspect are the default. Execute needs a workflow name and a person. Deploy needs a second yes. Applicant, resident, owner, and vendor messages stay in innflow.

Worked example: the pet addendum field

The packet workflow is deployed. Leasing wants a pet addendum flag on the input. The checklist in the repo does not mention it yet. Production logs from last week show the old input shape.

  1. Ask Cursor to inspect the deployed packet workflow and list inputs.
  2. Ask it to show one recent successful execution so you can see a real payload, not a guessed one.
  3. Edit the checklist in the repo. Review the diff yourself.
  4. Change the canvas in innflow only when leasing has agreed the new field is required.
  5. Deploy that change as its own step, with its own idempotency key if you deploy through the API.
  6. Execute a single test applicant that leasing has marked as safe to retry. Read the new log.
  7. Leave the applicant email on the canvas.

A prompt that matches the first step: "Using the innflow connection, inspect the applicant packet workflow and quote its input fields. Do not deploy or execute." That is the tone of a sane innflow Cursor integration. Curiosity first, state change second.

Agent mode likes to be helpful and finish the whole list. Stop it between inspect and deploy. The gap is where a person looks at the canvas.

A runner for the cases that are not interactive

After the field exists, a small script can execute the deployed workflow for a batch leasing already approved. The script uses a key.

curl -X POST https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows/{workflowId}/execute \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: packet-2026-09-29-applicant-88" \
  -d '{"input":{"applicantId":"88","petAddendum":true}}'

Cursor can write this script. It should not embed the key. Read the key from the environment. On failure, store requestId and X-Request-Id with the applicant id so the next person can find the same error.

Expire the key. Revoke it if a debug log prints it. The settings page shows last used time, which is enough to see whether a forgotten runner is still alive.

When the call fails, and the other MCP direction

Unauthorized means the grant is missing. Finish OAuth. A read-only error means you are inspecting with the right role and you tried to write. Switch role only if that person should deploy. A draft error means the canvas was never deployed. An idempotency conflict means the key does not match this body. Look at the previous response before you send a new one.

There is also an outward connection. Settings: MCP servers plus an MCP node lets a workflow call tools on some other server. Use that when the packet workflow needs an outside tool. Use the Cursor connection when a person in the editor needs the packet workflow. Write both down in the runbook under different names.

AES-256 applies in transit and at rest. Customer content is not kept for model training. Private and VPC deployment stay available. The mcp.json entry does not change those terms.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. The check you can do this afternoon is smaller: the input list in Cursor matches the canvas, and the applicant still hears from leasing inside innflow.

A review ritual that survives agent mode

Cursor will try to finish the whole leasing change in one turn. The ritual is a set of stops. Stop after the input list. Stop after the sample execution. Stop after the checklist diff. Stop again before deploy. Say the stop out loud in the prompt so the transcript shows it.

Keep a short project rule file the editor already reads. Name the packet workflow. Say that inspect is allowed, execute needs the applicant id in the prompt, and deploy needs a second message from a person. Say that applicant email is sent from innflow. Repeat the rule when someone new clones the repo. The mcp.json file gets them the server. The rule gets them the manners.

Once a week, compare three artifacts: the input list from inspect, a real execution payload, and the checklist in git. They should describe the same fields. When they drift, the checklist is wrong or the canvas changed without a note. Fix the drift before the next applicant. An innflow Cursor integration that is not checked against a real payload becomes a confident guess.

Practice one refusal. Ask agent mode to execute while the workflow is a draft, on a sandbox workflow you control. Read the error together. Teams that have seen the refusal do not argue with it later, during a live tour day.

If two leasing coordinators share one workspace, agree who executes. The other person may inspect. Shared execute rights plus two open Cursor windows is how duplicate packets happen. Idempotency keys help only when both people use the same key scheme. Write the scheme down: applicant id, workflow slug, and the date.

At the end of the change, leave the canvas deployed state in the pull request description. Reviewers should see whether this diff also required a deploy. A merged checklist with an undeployed canvas is an incomplete change, even if the code looks finished.

A weekly audit you can finish in twenty minutes

Pick one afternoon. Open the repo and the canvas. Ask Cursor to list the workflows this project is allowed to call. The allowed list should be one or two names, written in the project rules. Extra names are a sign the grant is wider than the work.

For the packet workflow, copy the input fields from inspect into the audit note. Open the newest successful execution and copy the keys that were actually sent. Diff them against the checklist. Three columns, one row per field: documented, inspected, executed. A field in only one column is the week's fix. Do not start a new feature while a column is empty.

Read the last error, if there is one. Save the request id in the note. Say whether it was unauthorized, a draft, a read-only role, or an idempotency conflict. Those four are the ones this integration is built to produce. Any other error gets the request id and a person, not another prompt that hopes the next try works.

Check git history for .cursor/mcp.json. The diff should only ever show the server name and the URL. If a token appeared, even briefly, revoke the credential and scrub the history with the person who owns the repo. Then look at who still has OAuth access to the workspace. Remove anyone who left the leasing project.

End the audit by naming the sender. One role sends applicant messages from innflow. If the note says "the agent," the audit failed. Write the person's role, not a model name. That single line keeps an innflow Cursor integration from drifting into an unsupervised mailbox.

When the audit finds a drift, fix it in the same afternoon if you can. A field that exists on the canvas and not in git will be missed by the next applicant. A field that exists in git and not on the canvas will be sent into a workflow that drops it. Either gap is a leasing error waiting for a tour day. Write the fix as a checklist change, a canvas change, or both, and deploy only the canvas half with a witness. Then re-run the three-column check on that one field so the note shows it closed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does an innflow Cursor integration replace our property management system?

No. The property management system remains the system of record for units, leases, and money. innflow runs the workflows. Cursor is the editor and the MCP client.

Will agent mode run a draft if I ask nicely?

No. Execute requires a deployed workflow. Deploy it on the canvas, then call execute.

Is it safe to commit .cursor/mcp.json?

Yes, when the file contains only the server name and the innflow URL. It is not safe once a key or a bearer token is added. Keep those out of the repo.

Can Cursor email the applicant?

Do not give the session that send. The workflow prepares the packet. Leasing sends from innflow.

How do we avoid two packet runs for one applicant?

Bind the run to an idempotency key that includes the applicant and the date or the attempt. Reuse it only for an identical retry. Change the payload, change the key.

Name the workflow before you change it

Add the config. Sign in. Inspect the packet. Read one real execution. Then decide if today's field belongs in production. That sequence is the innflow Cursor integration doing the job property teams actually have.

Open app.innflow.ai/signup to start, or app.innflow.ai if the workspace is already there.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Use an innflow Codex integration to list, inspect, and run deployed property workflows from the terminal, with OAuth scopes and a person on the send step.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
A terminal agent still needs an operations system

A property team does not run on chat. It runs on packets, notices, vendor calls, and the record of who approved the last step. Codex is a strong place to do the file work around that operation: read a repo, edit a template, and keep a command history. An innflow Codex integration is how that terminal session reaches the workflows that already know the operation.

innflow is property operations software with AI workflows. Agents run on a visible canvas. The property management system stays the system of record. Codex does not become that system, and innflow does not become the editor. The integration is the handshake between them.

This guide covers what the connection can do, how to attach Codex to the hosted MCP server, when the public API is the better path, and a worked example for an application packet. A person still owns the message that leaves the building.

What Codex is doing in a property repo

OpenAI Codex, in the CLI and in the IDE extension, is a coding harness. It plans a change, edits files, and runs commands inside a project you trust. Property teams use that shape more often than a pure software company admits.

The repo might hold notice templates, a checklist for move-in, a script that exports owner statements, or the notes an engineer keeps next to a workflow. Codex is good at that local work. It can see the files, propose a diff, and stop when you say stop.

It cannot see a deployed workflow, an execution log, or the credential boundary of a workspace unless you connect it. Pasting a screenshot of the canvas into the terminal is a slow version of the same idea. The connection makes the question direct: which workflows exist, which one is deployed, and what did the last run do.

That is the whole point of an innflow Codex integration. The harness stays in the repo. The operation stays on the canvas, where status, handoff, and permissions are visible.

What the connection is allowed to do

innflow exposes two doors.

The hosted MCP server is for harnesses that speak the Model Context Protocol. The endpoint is https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp. It uses OAuth 2.1. There is no API key on this door. Codex opens a sign-in, you pick a workspace, and you approve scopes. Access is workspace-scoped and revocable.

Once that session is authorized, Codex can do the same class of work the public API exposes:

  • List workflows in the workspace
  • Inspect one workflow
  • Run a workflow that is already deployed
  • Deploy a workflow, or return it to draft
  • List executions
  • Read execution details and node logs

A workflow that is still a draft will not execute. Read-only members of a workspace cannot use write endpoints. Those two rules matter more than the transport.

The public API is the second door, for scripts, cron, and any client that should use a key instead of an interactive sign-in. The base URL is https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1. Keys are created under Settings: API Keys. They start with inf_sk_ and the full value is shown once. The OpenAPI document lives at https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/openapi.json.

Requests default to the personal workspace. Send X-Innflow-Workspace with an organization id when the work belongs to another workspace you can access. Create, import, duplicate, deploy, undeploy, and execute accept an Idempotency-Key header. The same key and the same request replay the saved response for 24 hours. The same key with a different body returns a conflict.

Connect Codex with MCP

Codex stores MCP servers in config.toml, shared by the CLI and the IDE extension. The user file is ~/.codex/config.toml. A trusted project can also carry .codex/config.toml.

Add the server from the CLI:

codex mcp add innflow --url https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp

Or write the block yourself:

[mcp_servers.innflow]
url = "https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp"

Start Codex in the property repo and ask it to list innflow tools. The first call should send you through innflow sign-in. Pick the workspace that owns the workflows, review the scopes, and approve. If the server answers before that approval, you will see an unauthorized response. That is the connection waiting for a person, which is the correct first state.

Confirm the server is present:

codex mcp list

Then ask a narrow question. "List the workflows in this innflow workspace" is a better first prompt than "run everything." You want to see names before anyone executes.

Keep secrets out of the repo. The OAuth grant lives with the Codex sign-in. Do not copy an inf_sk_ key into config.toml and commit it. If a key has already leaked, revoke it under Settings: API Keys and create a new one.

A short note in AGENTS.md helps the session stay inside the boundary: use the innflow server to list and inspect workflows, execute only a named deployed workflow, and never send resident, owner, or vendor messages from the terminal. The send step stays in innflow.

When the public API is the better door

MCP fits an interactive Codex session. A nightly job is a different shape. Nobody is sitting at the sign-in window at 2 a.m.

For that job, create a key with a real expiration. Thirty days is enough for a trial. Ninety days or one year fits a stable script. "Never" is available and should be rare. Store the key in the secret store the job already uses. Pass it only as Authorization: Bearer.

A list call looks like this:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows

An execute call is allowed only after deploy:

curl -X POST https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows/{workflowId}/execute \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: application-packet-2026-09-29-unit-12" \
  -d '{"input":{"applicantEmail":"applicant@example.com"}}'

The response includes the workflow id, event ids, and a triggered status. Failures return JSON with a human-readable error, an optional code, and a requestId. The X-Request-Id header is the value to hand to support.

Use the API from Codex when the session is writing a script. Use MCP when the session is the operator. Mixing them in one prompt, with a key pasted into chat, is how keys leak.

Worked example: the application packet

A leasing coordinator finishes a tour. The applicant exists in the property management system. What the team still does by hand is the packet: pull the checklist, confirm the documents the workflow expects, and prepare the internal handoff. That packet is a deployed innflow workflow. The coordinator's engineer keeps the checklist copy in a repo Codex can read.

The session starts with inspection, not execution.

  1. Ask Codex to list workflows and name the application-packet workflow.
  2. Ask it to inspect that workflow so the required input fields are visible.
  3. Compare those fields to the checklist in the repo. If a field is missing, stop. Fix the input or the canvas. Do not execute a half-built payload.
  4. When the fields match, ask Codex to execute the deployed workflow with one applicant's input and a fresh idempotency key.
  5. Ask it to read the execution log. The log is the record. A cheerful summary is not.
  6. The person who owns leasing sends any applicant-facing message from innflow.

A prompt that respects the boundary sounds like this: "Using the innflow connection, inspect the deployed application packet workflow. Tell me the input fields. Do not execute yet." The second prompt, after a person agrees, names the workflow id and the input. The third prompt reads the new execution.

If Codex offers to email the applicant from the terminal, decline. Drafts can be prepared inside the workflow. The send stays on the canvas, where the credential and the handoff are visible.

Deploy is a separate decision. An innflow Codex integration can deploy, and it can return a workflow to draft. In the packet example, deploy belongs to the person who reviewed the canvas change. The terminal session can prepare the diff in the repo and can read logs. It should not ship a new version because the model sounded confident.

Controls, failures, and the other direction

Treat the connection like a staff login with a narrow job.

  • Approve the smallest workspace that contains the workflows this repo should see.
  • Prefer read prompts until the workflow name and the input shape are confirmed.
  • Execute only deployed workflows.
  • Put a new idempotency key on every real run. Reuse a key only when you intend to replay the same request.
  • Revoke the OAuth grant or the API key when a person leaves the repo or the role changes.

Common failures are ordinary. Unauthorized means the sign-in is not finished or the grant was revoked. A write rejected for a read-only member means the workspace role is doing its job. An execute rejected because the workflow is not deployed means the canvas is still a draft. An idempotency conflict means the key was reused with a different body. Read requestId before you retry.

There is a second direction, and it is easy to confuse with this one. Inside innflow, Settings: MCP servers registers an external MCP server, and an MCP node on the canvas can call that server's tools. That is innflow reaching out. An innflow Codex integration, as this guide uses the phrase, is Codex reaching in. Use the outward node when a workflow needs a tool Codex is not providing. Use the inward connection when a person in Codex needs the workflow.

Security on the innflow side stays in force either way. Traffic and stored data use AES-256. Model training does not retain customer data. Teams that need a private or VPC deployment can keep that boundary. The harness does not widen it.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. The useful proof in this setup is quieter: the canvas shows the flow, the log shows the run, and a person still releases anything a resident will read.

A first week that stays small

Day one is the connection and nothing else. Add the MCP server, finish OAuth, and ask Codex to list workflow names. Write those names into the repo note. If the list is empty, you are in the wrong workspace. Fix that before anyone talks about execution.

Day two is one old log. Pick a workflow the team already trusts and read a finished execution. Compare the input in the log with the checklist in the repo. Differences belong in the note. They are not a reason to execute a new run.

Day three is a single execute, on a case a person has marked as safe. Use a fresh idempotency key. Read the new log in the same session and again on the canvas. If the two views disagree, stop and keep the request id.

Day four is a failure drill. Ask Codex what an undeployed workflow does, and what a read-only member can do. You want to see the refusal. A session that cannot show you a refusal is a session you should not trust with a real packet.

Day five is the runbook paragraph: which workflow id, who may execute, who sends, and where the key lives if a script exists. That paragraph is the innflow Codex integration after the novelty wears off. The following week repeats day three. It does not add a second workflow until the first one has been boring.

Keep the API key, if you created one for a script, on a 30-day or 90-day expiration for this trial. Revoke it at the review even if you plan to create another. A key that survives its experiment becomes an unknown client.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does an innflow Codex integration replace our property management system?

No. The property management system remains the system of record. innflow runs the workflows around that record. Codex edits files and calls those workflows. Leases, ledgers, and units stay where they already live.

Can Codex execute a workflow that is still a draft?

No. Deploy the workflow on the canvas first. The API and the MCP session both refuse to execute a draft. That is the gate that keeps a terminal experiment off a live packet.

Should I paste an API key into Codex?

Use the hosted MCP sign-in for interactive sessions. Create an inf_sk_ key only for a script or a job, store it outside the repo, and revoke it if it appears in a prompt, a commit, or a log.

Can Codex email residents, owners, or vendors?

Do not give it that job. A workflow may prepare a draft. The person responsible sends it from innflow, on the credential the workspace already trusts.

What if two Codex sessions run the same packet?

Give each real run its own idempotency key. If a retry is truly the same request, reuse the key and innflow will replay the saved response for 24 hours instead of starting a second run.

Start with one deployed workflow

Pick the workflow your team already trusts. Connect Codex. List it. Inspect it. Read one old execution before you execute a new one. That sequence is the innflow Codex integration in practice: a terminal harness, a visible workflow, and a person on the step that leaves the building.

When the packet path is boring, add the next workflow. Boring is the goal.

Get started at app.innflow.ai/signup, or open the workspace you already have at app.innflow.ai. API details are in the innflow API introduction.
